INSURANCE ACT, 2021(ACT 1061)
INSURERS DIRECTIVE, 2024
The National Insurance Commission issues this directive under the powers granted
to it by section 198 of the Insurance Act, 2021.
PART 1 PRELIMINARY
Interpretation
1. In this directive, unless the context otherwise requires,
“accepting insurer” means a direct insurer that enters into a facultative
reinsurance contract, as reinsurer, with another direct insurer;
“Act” means the Insurance Act, 2021(Act 1061);
“agent-branded insurance product” means an insurance contract which is
marketed and sold under the branding of a licensed insurance agent,
rather than the branding of the licensed insurer that is underwriting
the contract;
“alternative risk transfer arrangement” has the meaning specified in
paragraph 58;
“associated company” has the meaning specified in paragraph 3;
“beneficiary”, in relation to an insurance contract, means any person
other than the policyholder
(a) who is entitled to a payment or a benefit under the insurance
contract; or
(b) who, on the occurrence of the insured event, is entitled to make
a claim against the insurer under the insurance contract;
“board” means the board of directors of a licensed insurer;
“branded product” means an agent branded product, a technical service
provider branded product or a co-branded product;
“bundled insurance product” has the meaning specified in paragraph 61;
“cedant” includes a reinsurer that transfers risk to another reinsurer under
a retrocession contract;
“chairperson” means the director appointed as the chairperson of the
board of a licensed insurer in accordance with paragraph 9(7);
“chief executive officer” means the employee of a licensed insurer who
is appointed as chief executive officer or who occupies an equivalent
position under a different name;
“chief finance officer” means the employee of a licensed insurer who is
appointed as chief finance officer or who occupies an equivalent
position under a different name;
“co-branded product” means an insurance contract which is marketed
and sold under the joint branding of the licensed insurer underwriting the
5

contract and either a licensed insurance agent or a licensed technical
service provider;
“complaint” in relation to a licensed insurer, means an oral or written
expression of dissatisfaction, whether justified or not, from or on behalf
of a person about the provision of a service which constitutes insurance
business and which
(a) alleges that the complainant has suffered, or may suffer,
financial loss, material distress or material inconvenience; and
(b) relates to the provision of the service by the insurer or on the
insurer’s behalf, including by its agents;
“customer information” includes information provided by or relating to
customers and prospective customers;
“day” means a calendar day;
“direct insurer” means an insurer the primary business of which is the
business of entering into direct insurance contracts;
“distribute”, in relation to a licensed insurer and an insurance contract,
has the meaning specified in paragraph 62;
“executive director” means a director of a licensed insurer who
(a) is an employee of the insurer; or
(b) not being an employee of the insurer, has day-to-day managerial
or operational responsibilities in relation to the insurer;
“facultative reinsurance” means the reinsurance of an individual risk or
a specified package of individual risks on the basis of an offer by the
cedant and acceptance by the reinsurer where
(a) the cedant is not under an obligation to offer the risks to the
reinsurer; and
(b) the reinsurer is not under an obligation to provide reinsurance;
“fronting arrangement” has the meaning specified in paragraph 56;
“independent director” means a non-executive director of a licensed
insurer who
(a) has not, at any time in the previous five years, been an executive
director or an employee of the insurer;
(b) is not a connected person in relation to the insurer;
(c) does not hold any shares or have any other interest in the insurer;
(d) does not receive any remuneration, commission or
compensation from the insurer other than remuneration as a
director; and
(e) does not have a material conflict of interest with the insurer;
“insurance product” means a single insurance contract or a bundled
insurance product;
6

“legal and regulatory obligation” means an obligation of a licensed
insurer under
(a) the Act, any Regulations made under the Act or the directives;
(b) applicable anti-money laundering and anti-terrorist financing
Acts, Regulations and directives; or
(c) any other Acts or Regulations relevant to its licensed business;
“licensed direct insurer” means a licensed insurer that is a direct insurer;
“life insurer” means a licensed insurer that is authorised by its licence to
carry on any class of life insurance business;
“life insurance business” means insurance business in any of the
following classes
(a) annuity business;
(b) life insurance; and
(c) investment linked life insurance;
“life insurance contract” means a contract of insurance in any class
specified in paragrahs (a) to (c) of the definition of “life insurance
business”;
“Lloyd’s” means the society of that name incorporated by Act of
Parlaiment of the United Kingdom known as Lloyd’s Act, 1871;
“Lloyd’s underwriter” means an underwriting member of Lloyd’s;
“long term insurance contract” means an insurance contract that falls
within any class of long term insurance business;
“net retention” means the amount of risk that a cedant retains, after taking
account of all reinsurance contracts entered into by the cedant in
relation to the risk concerned;
“non-executive director” means a director of a licensed insurer who is
not an executive director;
“outsourcing arrangement” means an arrangement between a licensed
insurer and a service provider under which the service provider, or
another person acting for the service provider, undertakes an activity
on a continuing basis that would normally be undertaken by the
insurer and “outsource” is to be construed accordingly;
“policyholder” in relation to an insurance contract, means the person who
entered into the insurance contract with the insurer or, if the rights
of that person under the contract have been assigned or transferred,
the person who has those rights;
“principal officer” means an employee of a licensed insurer who is
appointed
(a) as chief executive officer of the insurer;
(b) as chief finance officer of the insurer; or
7

(c) to undertake a senior management function approved by the
Commission;
“promotional material” includes any explanatory, advertising or
publicity material, in any form, including electronic form;
“retention” means the amount of risk that a cedant retains after entering
into a reinsurance or retrocession contract with respect to the risk;
“retrocessionaire” means a reinsurer that enters into a reinsurance
contract with a ceding reinsurer;
“risk appetite” means the aggregate level and types of risk a licensed
insurer is willing to assume within its risk capacity to achieve its
strategic objectives and business plan;
“service provider”, in relation to an outsourcing arrangement, means a
person who undertakes an activity for a licensed insurer under an
outsourcing arrangement with the insurer;
“significant complaint” has the meaning specified in paragraph 89; and
“technical service provider branded product” means an insurance
contract which is marketed and sold under the branding of a licensed
technical service provider, rather than the branding of the licensed insurer
that is underwriting the contract.
Application of this directive
2. (1) Unless stated otherwise or the context otherwise requires
(a) this directive applies to a licensed insurer and, with appropriate
modifications, to a licensed reinsurer; and
(b) a reference in the directive to a “licensed insurer” is taken to include
a reference to a licensed reinsurer.
Meaning of “associated company”
3. A company is an associated company in relation to another company if both
companies are in the same group of companies.
Connected persons
4. (1) This paragraph specifies additional circumstances in which one person is
connected to another person for the purposes of paragraph (c) of the definition of
“connected person” in section 259 of the Act.
(2) A person (the first person) is connected to another person (the second
person) in the following circumstances
(a) the second person is a company or any other undertaking where the
first person is a director, senior manager or key person in a control
function of the second person;
(b) both persons are partners of the same partnership; or
(c) the first person is a close family member of
(i) the second person, where that person is an individual;
(ii) an individual who is a significant owner of the second person;
or
8

(iii) an individual who is a director, senior manager or key person in
control function of the second person.
(3) For the purposes of subparagraph (2), “close family member”, in
relation to an individual, means the individual’s
(a) spouse or former spouse;
(b) children, including adopted children and step children;
(c) parents, including step parents;
(d) uncles and aunties
(e) legal guardian or former legal guardian;
(f) brothers and sisters, including step brothers and sisters;
(g) grandparents
(f) grandchildren; or
(g) cousin.
(4) The parents, brothers and sisters, including step brothers and sisters,
of a person’s spouse are also considered to be close family members of the
person.
Senior management functions
5. For the purposes of the definition of “senior management function” in section
259 of the Act
(a) an employee of a licensed insurer
(i) is answerable to the directors of the insurer if the employee
reports directly to the board with respect to any of the
employee’s management duties; and
(ii) has a responsibility that includes direct involvement in the
management or decision-making process of the insurer at a
senior level if the exercise of the responsibility involves, or
could involve, a risk of serious consequences for the insurer; and
(b) the following are considered to be key functions
(i) acting as chief finance officer or occupying an equivalent
position under a different name; and
(ii) acting as chief operations officer or occupying an equivalent
position under a different name.
Relationship with Commission
6. A licensed insurer must deal with the Commission in an open and cooperative
manner and must disclose to the Commission in a timely manner anything relating
to the insurer or its business of which the Commission would reasonably expect
notice.
9

GUIDELINES
Status and Purpose of Guidelines
1. These Guidelines are issued under section 201 of the Act. The Guidelines
should be read together with the directives and are intended to assist licensed
insurers by
(a) providing relevant background or explanatory information;
(b) setting out the factors that the Commission will take into account in
considering whether or not a requirement in the Act, the Regulations or
the directives has been complied with; and
(c) providing guidance on how the Commission expects licensed insurers
and others to comply with the Act, the Regulations and the directives.
2. The Guidelines are not part of the directives and do not have the force of law.
Although any failure to follow the Guidelines does not, in itself, render a
person liable to enforcement action or proceedings of any kind, the
Commission may take the failure into account in determining whether there
has been a contravention of the Act or the Regulations, and by extension, the
directives [see section 201(3) of the Act].
International Standards
3. The Commission is a member of the International Association of Insurance
Supervisors (IAIS) and, to the extent relevant and appropriate, applies the
Insurance Core Principles issued by the IAIS (the “ICPs”). The directives,
and the Guidelines, have been drafted taking into account the ICPs as
updated in November 2019 and other relevant standards and documents
published by the IAIS.
Definitions
4. Any words and terms that are defined in the Act bear the same meaning in
this directive and these Guidelines.
5. Independent director: One of the criteria for an “independent director” is
that the director does not have a material conflict of interest with the insurer.
A conflict of interest may be actual, potential or perceived. Materiality will
depend on the circumstances of the case, but the Commission considers that
any conflict having the potential to influence a director’s vote, or that could
be perceived by an outsider as having that potential, should always be
considered material. There may be instances in which a director has a
technical conflict of interest, but the conflict is most unlikely to influence any
vote that may be required in relation to the interest. For example, if a director
of a licensed insurer is a large shareholder of a company which is a customer
or supplier of the insurer, the conflict of interest will be material as the
outcome of any vote has the potential to impact on the benefit received by the
director. However, if the customer or supplier is a company with a significant
number of shares (for example a publicly listed company), the ownership by
the director of a small number of shares is unlikely to be material as the
10

benefit accruing to the director from any decision to enter a contract with the
company is likely to be insignificant. These are examples only. The
Commission expects a sensible and pragmatic view to be taken in any case
but also considers that, when in doubt, licensed insurers should consider
conflicts to be material.
6. Senior management function: This term is defined in section 259 of the Act.
The definition states that a person having responsibility for a control function
is not part of senior management. This is an important distinction as, given
the monitoring role played by the control functions, the ICPs require that:
(a) a licensed insurer’s control functions must be independent of those
persons responsible for the day-to-day management of the insurer; and
(b) the key person responsible for each control function should not have
operational business line responsibilities.
7. The Act provides that an employee who “holds a position that requires that
employee to be answerable to the directors of the licensee” has a senior
management function. All employees of a licensed insurer could be said to be
indirectly answerable to the directors through the management chain. That is
plainly not the intention of the Act. Paragraph 5(a)(i) of the directive
therefore amplifies the definition by indicating that the employee would need
to answer directly to the board with respect to the employee’s management
duties.
8. Paragraph (c) of the definition in the Act refers to a “key function” but does
not define the term. Paragraph 5(b) of the directive provides that acting as
chief finance officer or chief operations officer (or equivalent) are considered
key functions. This is not intended to be an exclusive list of positions.
Depending upon the circumstances, other positions or responsibilities could
be key functions.
9. Finally, paragraph (d) of the Act’s definition refers to management or
decision-making at a senior level. Paragraph 5(a)(ii) of the directive
indicates circumstances in which an employee would be considered to act at
a senior level, i.e., that the exercise of the responsibilities involves, or could
involve, a risk of serious consequences for the licensed insurer. This does not
limit the definition in the Act.
Relationship with the Commission
10. The legal and regulatory framework contains a number of requirements,
including the submission of documents and returns to the Commission on a
regular basis and if triggered by certain specific events or changes in
circumstances. A licensed insurer is also required to disclose anything
related to the insurer or its business of which the Commission would
reasonably expect notice. The Commission considers that this includes any
matter that might reasonably be expected to materially affect the
Commission’s regulation and supervision of the insurer. Compliance with
this obligation requires a licensed insurer not just to respond to the specific
requirements of the Act and directives, but also to be proactive in supplying
the Commission with information, when appropriate.
11

PART 2 – GOVERNANCE AND RISK MANAGEMENT
Governance
Governance framework
7. (1) A licensed insurer must take reasonable care to organise and control its
affairs effectively, taking into account the nature, scale, complexity and diversity
of its business and the risks to which it is exposed, and establish and maintain
(a) the strategies, policies, procedures and controls required by the Act
and the directives; and
(b) adequate and effective risk management strategies, policies,
procedures and controls.
(2) The governance framework must include
(a) an adequate and transparent organisational structure;
(b) an effective system for the transmission of information;
(c) policies that clearly define and support the objectives of the licensed
insurer; and
(d) requirements relating to
(i) how decisions and actions are taken; and
(ii) the documentation of material decisions and actions, including
their rationale.
(3) A licensed insurer must ensure that the strategies, policies,
procedures and controls are fully and clearly documented and are
communicated, as appropriate, to senior management, key persons in control
functions and other relevant employees.
(3) The strategies, policies, procedures and controls must specify the
duties and responsibilities of the board and senior management, including such
responsibilities and duties as are imposed on the board and senior management
by the Act, the directives and any other laws.
(4) If a licensed insurer is part of a group, the strategies, policies,
procedures and controls required by this Act and the directives must include
group-wide strategies, policies, procedures and controls.
Allocation of responsibilities
8. In apportioning significant responsibilities between the board, board
committees, senior managers and key persons in a control function in compliance
with section 74(1)(a) of the Act, the board of a licensed insurer must ensure that
significant responsibilities are
(a) clearly defined;
(b) allocated to
(i) the board or board committees, where appropriate; or
(ii) persons who have been approved by the Commission as
directors, senior managers or key persons in a control function,
as appropriate for the significant responsibility concerned; and
12

(c) identify the person or persons who
(i) are accountable for the discharge of each significant
responsibility; and
(ii) possess the legal duties and powers to act on behalf of the
insurer and under which circumstances.
Board of directors
9. (1) A licensed insurer must ensure that on appointment and thereafter on an
ongoing basis
(a) its directors are fit and proper;
(b) the board has, and maintains, a sufficient number of members who,
collectively, have an adequate spread of relevant knowledge, skills,
and experience in the fields of insurance, actuarial science, risk
management, audit, law, finance, accounting, economics,
investment management, business administration, or related courses
and a sufficient understanding of
(i) the business of the licensed insurer; and
(ii) the risks to which the licensed insurer is exposed,
to enable the board to fulfil its responsibilities effectively.
(2) In determining whether a person to be appointed director and, on an
ongoing basis each director, has sufficient time and commitment to undertake
the duties of a director, a licensed insurer must take into account
(a) any other directorships that the person or director holds; and
(b) the scope of the duties and responsibilities associated with each of
those directorships.
(3) The board of a licensed insurer is responsible for monitoring the
sufficiency and independence of its members.
(4) Without limiting subparagraph (1)(b), a licensed insurer must have
(a) at least seven directors, one of whom must be the chief executive
officer; and
(b) sufficient non-executive directors to ensure that more than half the
members of the audit committee are non-executive directors.
(5) A licensed insurer must ensure that
(a) at least one third in number of the board members, rounded up to the
nearest whole number, are citizens of Ghana;
(b) at least one third in number of the board members, rounded up to the
nearest whole number, are persons resident in Ghana;
(c) at least one third in number of the board members, rounded up to the
nearest whole number, are independent, non-executive directors;
and
(d) at least one third number of the board members, rounded down to
the nearest whole number, are women.
13

(6) A director who is both a citizen of Ghana and a resident of Ghana
may be counted for the purposes of subparagraph (4)(a) and (b).
(7) The board of a licensed insurer shall ensure that
(a) each newly appointed non-executive director is provided with
adequate induction training concerning the operations and
performance of the insurer; and
(b) adequate on-going training is provided to all directors and that the
training is updated as necessary.
(c) each non-executive director
(i) receives approved corporate governance training from the
Ghana Insurance College in each calendar year; and
(ii) provides the licensed insurer with a certificate issued by the
Ghana Insurance College evidencing successful completion of
the training within one month of completion of the training.
(8) A licensed insurer must ensure that one of the directors is appointed
as chairperson.
(9) The director appointed as chairperson must be a non-executive
director and must not serve as
(a) the chief executive officer; or
(b) the chairperson of any board committee.
(10) Either the chief executive officer or the chairperson, or both the chief
executive officer and the chairperson, must be a citizen of, and resident in,
Ghana.
(11) The board of a licensed insurer shall ensure that, at all times, a board
secretary is appointed.
(12) The board secretary, who is not required to be a director, has the
following responsibilities
(a) arranging meetings of the board;
(b) keeping records and minutes of board meetings;
(c) keeping records of board resolutions;
(d) keeping a register of directors’ interests; and
(e) perform any other functions assigned by the board.
(13) If, at any time, the insurer does not comply with any subparagraph
of this paragraph, it must
(a) immediately give the Commission written notice of its non–
compliance; and
(b) within a period not exceeding twenty-one days from the date that it
first failed to comply, submit to the Commission an application for
approval to appoint sufficient directors to bring it back into
compliance with the subparagraph concerned.
(14) The following transition provisions apply
14

(a) subparagraph (5)(d) takes effect on the transition date;
(b) a licensed insurer shall take reasonable steps to progressively
implement the requirements of subparagraph (5)(d) during the
transition period; and
(c) for the purposes of this subparagraph
(i) the transition date is 1 October 2030; and
(ii) the transition period is the period from the date that this directive
comes into force and the transition date.
Term limits for directors
10. (1) A person is not qualified for appointment as a non-executive director of
a licensed insurer if the person
(a) has been a director of the insurer for an aggregate period of more
than five years and the person’s continued appointment as director
has not been approved by the shareholders by a resolution passed at
a general meeting; or
(b) has been a director of the insurer for an aggregate period of more
than 10 years.
(2) A person is not qualified for appointment as an executive director of
a licensed insurer if the person has been a director of the insurer for an
aggregate period of more than 12 years.
(3) Subparagraph (1) does not apply to a non-executive director who
holds more than 10% of the issued shares of the licensed insurer.
(4) The following transitional provisions apply
(a) a person who on the transition date had served as the chief executive
officer of a licensed insurer for a period exceeding twelve years may
continue to serve as chief executive officer and as an executive
director until 30 September 2026;
(b) a person who on the transition date had served as the chief executive
officer of a licensed insurer for a period of seven years or more may
continue to serve as chief exceutive officer and as an executive
diretor for a total period of 17 years from the date of first
appointment as chief executive officer;
(c) subparagraph (2) does not apply to a person who on the transition
date
(i) was the chief executive officer of the licensed insurer; and
(ii) held more than 10% of the issued shares of the licensed insurer,
provided that the person continues to satisfy the conditions specified
in subparagraphs (i) and (ii).
(5) For the purposes of subparagraph (4), the transition date is 1 October
2021.
(6) The following directives are repealed
15

(a) the Directive on Term Limits for Directors and Managing Directors
(NIC/CIR/03/21/RN/HOS);
(b) the Directive on Term Limits for Directors and Chief Executive
Officers (NIC/CIR/12/21/RN/HOS).
Board powers and resources
11. (1) A licensed insurer must ensure that the board has
(a) sufficient and adequate powers; and
(b) access to adequate human and non-human resources,
to enable it to properly discharge its functions and responsibilities.
(2) The powers of the board must include the powers to
(a) obtain timely and comprehensive information relating to the
management of the insurer; and
(b) direct access to senior managers, key persons in a control function
and other relevant persons.
Duties of individual directors
12. (1) A director of a licensed insurer, when acting as a director, has the
following duties
(a) to act in good faith, honestly and reasonably;
(b) to exercise due care and diligence;
(c) to act in the best interests of the licensed insurer and policyholders,
putting those interests ahead of the director’s own interests;
(d) to exercise independent and objective judgment, taking the interests
of the licensed insurer and policyholders into account; and
(e) not to use the position of director to gain undue personal advantage.
(2) A licensed insurer must ensure that the duties set out in subparagraph
(1) are
(a) specified in the terms of appointment of each director; or
(b) otherwise agreed to in writing by each director.
Principal responsibilities of the board
13. (1) The board of a licensed insurer has the following responsibilities
(a) ensuring that the licensed insurer
(i) establishes and maintains a governance framework complying
with the Act and this directive;
(ii) has adequate senior management staff and other employees with
the skills, knowledge and expertise necessary for the discharge
of the responsibilities allocated to them and that the skills
knowledge and expertise of senior management remain
appropriate given the nature, scale, complexity and diversity
of the business of the licensed insurer and the risks to which it
is exposed;
16

(iii) establishes the required control functions and appoints suitable
individuals as key persons in those control functions;
(iv) establishes, maintains and implements appropriate and effective
procedures and controls for giving effect to the licensed
insurer’s strategies and policies, including internal controls and
procedures and controls with respect to risk management;
(v) complies with its legal and regulatory obligations;
(b) setting, reviewing and exercising effective oversight at least on an
annual basis
(i) the business objectives and the licensed insurer’s strategy for
achieving its business objectives;
(ii) the risk management strategy; and
(iii) the corporate culture and values;
(c) ensuring that the business objectives and strategies for achieveing
them take account of the the long term financial safety and
soundeness of the insurer and the interests of policyholders;
(d) setting, approving and reviewing on at least an annual basis the
licensed insurer’s significant strategies, policies, procedures and
controls;
(e) ensuring that the business objectives, strategies and corporate
culture and values are fully and clearly documented and are
communicated, as appropriate, to senior management, key persons
in control functions and other relevant employees;
(f) ensuring that it has effective oversight of senior management;
(g) monitoring
(i) the implementation of the risk management and other strategies,
policies, procedures and controls, including internal controls;
(ii) whether the strategies, policies, procedures and controls are
operating effectively and as intended; and
(iii) the management of the licensed insurer by senior management
in accordance with the strategies and policies set or approved by
the board and the risk appetite and corporate culture of the
licensed insurer;
(h) setting clear and objective performance goals for the licensed
insurer, and for senior management, periodically monitoring
performance against those goals and assessing their continued
relevance and appropriateness;
(i) ensuring that the licensed insurer establishes and maintains policies
relating to the engagement, dismissal and succession of senior
management;
(j) setting documented standards for business conduct and ethical
behaviour for directors, senior management and other employees;
17

(k) ensuring that the licensed insurer has reliable financial reporting

GUIDELINES
Corporate Governance
11. Corporate governance describes the way in which a company is controlled
and managed and is critical to the success of an insurer. The G20/OECD
“Principles of Corporate Governance” defines corporate governance as
involving:
21

“A set of relationships between a company’s management, its board, its
shareholders and other stakeholders. Corporate governance also provides
the structure through which the objectives of the company are set, and the
means of attaining those objectives and monitoring performance are
determined.”
The Commission considers this to be a good working definition for the
insurance sector in Ghana.
The primary participants are the board of directors, including board
committees, senior management, persons who have specific control functions
and persons. It is essential that a licensed insurer has a strong corporate
governance framework that sets out the roles and responsibilities of the
various participants and specifies how they inter-relate.
12. Objectives: An effective corporate governance framework enables an insurer
to be flexible and transparent; to be responsive to developments affecting its
operations in making timely decisions and to ensure that powers are not
unduly concentrated. The corporate governance framework supports and
enhances the ability of the key players responsible for an insurer’s corporate
governance; i.e., the board, senior management and key persons in control
functions to manage the insurer’s business soundly and prudently.
Governance Framework
13. Section 74(1)(a) of the Act requires that the governance framework of a
licensed insurer must provide for a “clear and appropriate apportionment of
significant responsibilities between directors, senior managers and key
persons in control functions”. In relation to directors, the apportionment of
responsibilities applies to the board as a whole and to apportionment between
committees and individual directors, if appropriate. In relation to senior
management, the Commission considers that responsibilities assigned to
senior management and key persons in control functions are allocated to
specific persons who have been approved for appointment by the Commission
and that the responsibilities are consistent with the roles or functions for
which they have been approved. The Commission will also need to be satisfied
that
(a) there is adequate separation for effective management and oversight;
and
(b) powers are not unduly concentrated.
The governance framework should also set out how directors, senior
management and key persons in control functions will be held accountable.
If responsibilities are allocated to more than one individual, the governance
framework must clearly show how the responsibilities are shared or divided
between the individuals concerned and how the person or persons will be
accountable for the performance of those responsibilities.
14. The written record required by section 74(5) of the Act may comprise different
types of documents including, for example, organigrams, project
management documents, job descriptions, committee constitutions and terms
of reference provided that all relevant documents are identified, the
22

organisational structure is transparent and that, taken together, the different
documents
(a) show the structure of the board, any board committees, senior
management and key persons in control functions and define the duties
and responsibilities of each and their reporting lines; and
(b) enable compliance with the Act and the directives.
Strategies, Policies, Procedures and Controls
15. The most critical strategies, policies, procedures and controls for a licensed
insurer are
(a) its risk management strategies, policies, procedures and controls; and
(b) its internal controls.
16. In broad terms, a licensed insurer should have
(a) strategies that set out the approach of the licensed insurer for dealing
with specific areas of risk and specific legal and regulatory obligations
and requirements;
(b) policies that set out the way in which the strategies will be implemented
by senior management and other employees by defining specific
requirements which they must follow;
(c) detailed procedures for the implementation of the strategies and
policies; and
(d) controls to ensure that the strategies, policies and procedures are in
place, are being observed or implemented and are effective in meeting
the intended objectives.
17. Paragraph 13(1)(b) of the directive requires the board to review the business
objectives and strategy on at least an annual basis. The Commission expects
the board to undertake more frequent reviews if, for example
(a) there are significant changes in the insurer’s business;
(b) it introduces new types or classes of risk, whether due to the
introduction of new types of products or decisions to market to different
categories of customer; or
(c) internal or external events occur that may significantly impact the
insurer.
Board
18. Referencing paragraph 9 of the directive:
(a) The objective of subparagraph (1)(a) is to ensure that the directors are
fit, individually and collectively. The Commission does not expect all
directors to possess knowledge, skills, understanding and experience in
all facets of the business, but the Commission does expect that the board
determines the knowledge, skills, understanding and experience needed
and ensures that the board as a whole possesses them.
23

(b) The objective of subparagraph (5)(d) is to accelerate progress
towards a better gender balance on the boards of licensed insurers. Gender
balanced boards have the potential to improve the performance of licensed
insurers. Licensed insurers that do not have the required number of women
on their boards should be mindful of the term limits of their existing directors
with the view to replacing retiring directors with women when their term of
appointment expires.
19. A person to be appointed by a licensed insurer as a director may hold other
directorships in Ghana and/or foreign companies). While this does not
necessarily mean that the person should not be appointed as a director, the
number of other directorships held, and the scope of the person’s duties and
responsibilities under each of those directorships, is relevant to the time and
commitment that the person is able to give to the licensed insurer and,
possibly, to conflict of interest.
20. The board of a licensed insurer should pay particular attention to the conflict
of interest risks associated with cross directorships. These arise when a
person acts as a director for more than one entity that operates within the
insurance sector or the wider financial services sector, whether within or
outside Ghana. Within the insurance sector, a director may serve on the
board of only one life insurance company and one non-life insurance
company at the same time.
21. The key is transparency and disclosure. It is therefore essential that the board
of a licensed insurer is aware of all directorships, in or outside Ghana, held
by an individual that it is considering appointing as a director. The board
will then be in a position to assess the risk of a conflict of interest and to act
accordingly. Where the board determines that there is a conflict of interest it
may decide not to make the appointment or, if it considers that the conflict
can be managed, making the appointment subject to appropriate conditions.
The board of a licensed insurer should also ensure that, at a minimum, its
directors disclose all directorships on an ongoing basis.
22. The Commission therefore expects a licensed insurer to satisfy itself that it
has obtained details of all other directorships held by a person to be
appointed as a director, that it understands the nature and extent of the
person’s responsibilities under each of the other directorships and to take this
into account when determining whether the person has sufficient time and
commitment to undertake the duties of a director diligently as required by
section 75(1)(c) of the Act.
23. Other directorships to which a person is appointed after becoming a director
of the licensed insurer will be relevant to the ongoing fit and proper
assessment required by paragraph 9(1) of the directive.
24. Non-executive directors, as they are not involved with the day-to day
operations of an insurer, can be more independent and objective in decision
making. The board is responsible for ensuring a balance between executive
and non-executive directors to enable appropriate objective and independent
decision-making.
25. An effective board is critical to sound governance and to the success of an
insurer. Paragraph 9 sets out the minimum requirements in relation to the
24

composition of the board necessary for it to fulfil its role effectively. The
failure of an insurer to meet these requirements could suggest a more
significant failure in governance or of the insurer itself. The Commission
therefore expects an insurer to notify the Commission of any contravention of
paragraph 9.
Term Limits for directors
26. Paragraph 10 of this directive replaces the directives issued by the
Commission on 30 July and 1 October 2021. The transition date of 1 October
2021 is the date on which the second directive was issued. As this paragraph
effectively replaces the earlier directives, which are repealed, the provisions
have continuous effect from that date.
Duties of Individual Directors
27. Section 190 of the Companies Act, 2019 provides for the statutory duties and
responsibilities of directors of all companies. Paragraph 12 of the directive
therefore sets out a comprehensive list of the duties of an individual director.
The Commission expects the duties of the directors of an insurer to be
incorporated in the terms of engagement of each director.
Responsibilities of the Board
28. The board is responsible for providing the overall strategy and direction for
an insurer and overseeing its overall management, leaving the day-to-day
management of the insurer to senior management. In order to provide
effective oversight of senior management, it is important that the board of
directors meet regularly with senior management to review the decisions
taken, the information provided, and the explanations given by senior
management. Responsibility for the oversight of senior management should
rest primarily with the non-executive directors as they do not have any
responsibilities for the day-to-day management of the insurer.
29. The corporate culture and values should require responsible and ethical
behaviour of all employees of an insurer and should not allow behaviour that
that would be incompatible with the protection of customers or that could
lead to reputational risks or improper or illegal activity, such as financial
misreporting, fraud, money laundering, bribery and corruption. It is
important that employees understand that unacceptable behaviour will lead
to appropriate disciplinary action.
30. Paragraph 13(1)(j) of the directive requires the board to set documented
standards for business conduct and ethical behaviour. The Commission
expects that the standards set will encourage a strong risk culture and
prohibit excessive risk taking. The paragraph requires the standards to be
documented. The Commission expects insurers to comply with this
requirement by approving a Code of Conduct, or similar document, which the
directors, senior management and all employees must observe.
31. The Commission expects the corporate culture to promote and facilitate
timely and frank discussion and escalation of problems to either senior
management or the board.
25

32. Paragraph 13(3)(b) of the directive requires the board to review its own
performance periodically. Where weaknesses or areas that could be
improved are identified, the Commission expects the board to develop and
implement a plan to address the weaknesses or areas for improvement. The
primary objective of the external review is to enhance the objectivity and
integrity of the board’s own assessment process.
33. Although the requirement is for at least an annual review, the Commission
expects the board to undertake more frequent reviews if circumstances
require. For example, material changes in an insurer’s business or external
events that may significantly affect the insurer may justify an ad hoc review.
Board Committees
34. The effect of paragraph 15 of the directive is to require that board committees
have clearly defined mandates and working procedures (including reporting
to the Board), authority to carry out their respective functions, and that the
individual directors appointed to a committee, together with each committee
have the degree of independence and objectivity appropriate to the
committee’s role. The Board should consider occasional rotation of members
and chairpersons of committees, or tenure limits to serve on a committee, as
this can help to avoid undue concentration of power and promote fresh
perspectives.
35. The board committees specified in paragraph 15(1) and (2) are the absolute
minimum that a licensed insurer must have. The board should consider
whether other committees are warranted. The Commission considers that
most insurers will also have a human resources committee and a finance
committee. If not established, the Commission will expect the board, if asked,
to justify their decision of not establishing them.
36. The board remains ultimately responsible for matters delegated to a
committee. It is therefore important that the Board as a whole, has regular
interaction with board committees and that it adopts a proactive approach to
seeking information from the committees, as well as from senior management.
Remuneration Policy
37. The Commission expects the remuneration policies required under
paragraph 18 of this directive to balance the need for discouraging excessive
risk-taking and promoting the fair treatment of customers and potential
customers with the ability of the licensed insurer to attract and retain
competent and experienced staff. Where appropriate, the Commission
expects the remuneration policy to cover, and take account of, performance
based variable structures and the balance of fixed and variable components,
performance criteria and any potential conflicts arising. The Commission
considers that if a licensed insurer establishes a remuneration committee, it
would be desirable for the relevant key persons in control functions to be
seconded to the committee in an advisory capacity.

Risk Management
Control functions
20. (1) The board of a licensed insurer must ensure that a control function
(a) is not involved in the performance of services or activities that it is
responsible for monitoring;
(b) is not placed in a position where it is expected to undertake duties
that conflict with its duties as control function;
(c) is not subjected to any undue influence or pressure with respect to
the carrying out of its duties as control function;
(d) is given sufficient status within the licensed insurer to ensure that
senior management and the board react to, and act on, its
recommendations;
(e) has such access as is required to undertake its duties as control
function effectively to
(i) every employee and service provider of the licensed insurer and,
where appropriate, to the board, the audit committee and the
internal audit function; and
(ii) documents and information relating to the business of the
licensed insurer and its customers; and
(f) has sufficient
(i) human resources with adequate professional qualifications,
relevant experience and training; and
(ii) non-human resources, including information technology and
management information systems;
to undertake the duties of the control function effectively.
(2) The authority and responsibilities of each control function, and the
key person in the control function, must be set out in writing.
(3) The board must ensure that the performance of each control function
is assessed at such intervals as the board considers appropriate.
Combining control functions
21.(1) Subject to subparagraphs (2) and (3), a licensed insurer may combine one
or more control functions.
(2) Notwithstanding subparagraph (1)
(a) the actuarial function must not be combined with any control
function other than the risk management function; and
(b) the internal audit function must not be combined with any other
control function.
(3) Control functions must not be combined unless the board is satisfied
that
27

(a) the combination of the functions will not affect the function’s
independence, objectivity or effectiveness;
(b) the combined function will comply with paragraph 20(1) and, in
particular
(i) the combined function will be sufficiently independent from
senior management; and
(ii) the combined function will be provided with sufficient resources
to fulfil the duties of each control function.
Key persons in control functions
22. (1) Subject to subparagraph (2), a licensed insurer must ensure that a key
person in a control function appointed under section 77(2)(b) of the Act is a suitably
experienced and senior employee of the licensed insurer or of a member of the same
group as the licensed insurer.
(2) Subparagraph (1) does not apply if the duties of the control function
are to be wholly outsourced to a service provider, as permitted by this directive.
(3) A licensed insurer must not appoint a person as the key person in a
control function unless
(a) it is satisfied that the person is fit and proper to be responsible for
that control function; and
(b) the Commission has given its approval for the appointment of that
person under section 55 of the Act.
(4) A licensed insurer must not appoint a person as the key person in a
control function and must not outsource a control function, or material aspects
of a control function, without the approval of the board or, where a board
committee has responsibility for the control function, without the approval of
that committee.
(5) If any control functions are combined, as permitted by paragraph 21,
the licensed insurer must appoint an individual to undertake the responsibilities
of, or have overall responsibility for and oversight of, the combined control
function and the individual appointed is regarded as the key person in each of
the combined control functions.
Risks to be provided for in risk management strategy, policy and procedures
23. (1) The board of a licensed insurer must ensure that the risk management
strategy, policies and procedures cover the identification and management of
(a) the risks specified in section 78(2)(d) of the Act;
(b) legal risk;
(c) reputational risk;
(d) conduct of business risk; and
(e) such other risks as the board may identify as material risks in
accordance with subparagraphs (2) and (3).
(2) The board of a licensed insurer must determine whether, given the
nature, scale, complexity and diversity of its business, any reasonably
28

foreseeable and relevant material risks not specified in subparagraph (1)(a) to
(c) should be covered by the risk management system.
(3) Without limiting subparagraph (2), the board should, in particular,
consider whether any of the following risks should be covered by the risk
management system
(a) contagion risk;
(b) pricing and product design risk;
(c) reinsurance risk;
(d) outsourcing risk;
(e) foreign exchange risk; and
(f) cyber risk.
Risk management strategy and policies of a licensed insurer
24. (1) The risk management strategy, policies, procedures and controls of a
licensed insurer must
(a) set the level of risk that the licensed insurer is prepared to accept for
each type of risk (its risk appetite) and, where appropriate, authority
levels for employees;
(b) be approved, and reviewed at least annually by the board; and
(c) be fully and clearly documented and effectively communicated and
readily available to the directors and to those members of senior
management and other employees and service providers who have
responsibility for implementing them.
(2) The board and senior management are responsible for
(a) ensuring that they understand all the risks to which the licensed
insurer is exposed in its business;
(b) assessing the resources required for an appropriate risk management
system, including accurate and reliable management information
and reporting procedures, and for ensuring that the required
resources are available; and
(c) overseeing the implementation of the risk management strategy,
policies, procedures and controls of the licensed insurer.
(3) Without limiting this paragraph, the risk management procedures and
controls of a licensed insurer must
(a) enable the licensed insurer to monitor the adequacy and
effectiveness of
(i) its risk management strategy and policies and their
implementation; and
(ii) measures taken to address any deficiencies identified in the risk
management strategy, policies, procedures and controls; and
29

(b) ensure that any exceptions to the risk management strategy and
policies of the licensed insurer are reviewed and authorised by senior
management and, where appropriate, the board.
Risk management function
25. (1) The principal duties of the risk management function are to
(a) assist the licensed insurer to identify, assess, monitor, manage and
report on its key risks in a timely manner; and
(b) promote and sustain a sound risk culture within the licensed insurer.
(2) A licensed insurer must require the key person in the risk
management function to report to the board any matter that may have an
adverse material impact on the risk management system of the licensed insurer,
as soon as reasonably practicable after identifying the matter.
Underwriting and pricing strategy, policies, procedures and controls
26. (1) A licensed insurer must establish and maintain
(a) an underwriting and pricing strategy;
(b) underwriting and pricing policies; and
(c) procedures and controls that are sufficient to ensure that the
underwriting and pricing strategy and policies are effectively
implemented.
(2) The issues provided for in the underwriting and pricing policies must
include
(a) the evaluation of risks underwritten or to be underwritten;
(b) subject to any minimum premium rates prescribed by the
Commission under section 256 of the Act, the establishment of
adequate premium levels;
(c) the mitigation and diversification of risks by
(i) defining limits on the amount of risk retained; and
(ii) in the case of a licensed insurer, providing for the transfer of
appropriate levels of risk away from the licensed insurer through
adequate and appropriate reinsurance arrangements made in
accordance with the provisions of the Act and the directives.
(3) Without limiting subparagraph (1)(b), the procedures and controls
must include controls of expenses related to premiums and claims.
(4) The underwriting and pricing strategy and the significant
underwriting and pricing policies must be approved, and reviewed
periodically, by the board.
(5) Senior management must monitor the procedures and controls
established in accordance with subparagraph (1)(b) on an ongoing basis.
Internal Controls
27. Establishment and maintenance of internal controls
30

(1) A licensed insurer must establish and maintain adequate and
effective internal controls appropriate for the nature, scale, complexity and
diversity of its business and the risks to which it is exposed.
(2) The internal controls must, as appropriate, operate at all levels of a
licensed insurer and must extend to any outsourced functions.
(3) Where a licensed insurer also operates through branches and
subsidiaries, its internal controls must extend to those operations and enable
effective oversight by the licensed insurer.
Matters to be covered by internal controls
28. (1) The internal controls of a licensed insurer must be designed to secure that
(a) the business of the licensed insurer is planned and conducted
properly and in accordance with
(i) the strategies and policies established by the board and any
policies established by senior management, including the
business objectives established by the board; and
(ii) the established procedures.
(b) the business of the licensed insurer is being operated in compliance
with its legal and regulatory obligations;
(c) the assets of the licensed insurer are appropriately safeguarded
through measures designed to minimise the risk of loss from
irregularities, error, fraud and physical damage, and to identify such
occurrences promptly should they occur;
(d) the liabilities of the licensed insurer are subject to appropriate
controls;
(e) there are appropriate arrangements in place for the delegation of
authority and responsibility and for the segregation of duties;
(f) the accounting and other records of the licensed insurer are
complete, accurate and timely and can be used to compile financial
statements as required by the regulatory enactments, management
information and returns to the Commission in line with the
obligations of the licensed insurer;
(g) the board and senior management are able to assess and monitor the
adequacy of the capital resources, in relation to the business of the
licensed insurer, including its risk profile and the quality of its
assets;
(h) the board and senior management are able to identify and regularly
assess all relevant risks in the conduct of the business of the licensed
insurer, so that
(i) identified risks can be measured, monitored and controlled
appropriately; and
(ii) any losses can be monitored and controlled on a regular and
timely basis.
31

(i) the board and senior management are able to identify, assess and
prevent or manage conflicts of interest, inlcuding related party
transactions;
(j) the board and senior management are able to guard properly against
involvement in financial crime and ensure that the licensed insurer
is complying with the anti–money laundering and terrorist financing
legislation;
(k) adequate business resumption, disaster recovery and other
contingency arrangements are in place and tested at appropriate
intervals; and
(l) adequate controls are in place in relation to information technology
systems, including controls that
(i) cover the key business, information technology and financial
policies and procedures and the related risk management and
compliance systems in place;
(ii) protect the accuracy and security of the information technology
systems;
(iii) restrict employees’ access to records unless access is required
for their roles and function;
(iv) ensure that changes to systems and records are recorded and that
only valid changes are made to them; and
(m) underwriting is carried out in accordance with the insurer’s
underwriting strategy and policies.
(2) The internal control policies must require any deficiencies identified
in the internal control system to be reported in a timely manner to senior
management and for material internal control deficiencies identified to be
reported to the board, even though they may have been corrected.
Responsibilities of board and senior management in relation to internal
controls
29. (1) The board of a licensed insurer has ultimate responsibility for ensuring
that adequate and effective internal controls are established and maintained.
(2) Without limiting subparagraph (1), the board must
(a) ensure that senior management
(i) implements the internal controls strategies and policies
established by the board; and
(ii) monitors the effectiveness of the internal controls of the licensed
insurer and its market conduct activities on an on-going basis;
(iii) makes regular reports to the board on the effectiveness of the
internal control system; and
(b) approve
(i) an appropriate organisational structure for the licensed insurer;
and
32

(ii) new products and major risk management initiatives.
(3) Senior management of a licensed insurer has the responsibility for
(a) implementing the strategy and policies of the board with respect to
internal controls;
(b) ensuring that
(i) the internal controls required by this directive are established
and maintained;
(ii) the required information systems are put in place; and
(iii) the internal controls are monitored, and deficiencies corrected,
as soon as reasonably practicable; and
(c) reviewing the internal controls at least annually and reporting the
results to the board.
Compliance function
30. (1) The principal duties of the compliance function of a licensed insurer are
(a) to assist the licensed insurer to meet, and to monitor its compliance
with, its legal and regulatory obligations;
(b) to promote and sustain a compliance culture within the licensed
insurer.
(2) For the purposes of subparagraph (1), the compliance function must
prepare a compliance procedure manual for the licensed insurer or, where the
preparation of the compliance procedures manual is outsourced, approve the
compliance procedure manual.
(3) The compliance function must, on behalf of the licensed insurer
(a) maintain a register of compliance breaches containing information
on the date, nature and extent of each compliance breach;
(b) ensure that employees are aware of the need for and the objectives
of compliance and of their responsibilities under the compliance
procedure manual, including by providing regular appropriate
training on the legal and regulatory obligations of the licensed
insurer;
(c) establish and maintain procedures for the monitoring and handling
of complaints and keeping the complaints procedures under review.
(4) The key person in the compliance function must report directly to the
board.
(5) A licensed insurer must require the key person in the compliance
function to report to the chairperson, as soon as reasonably practicable
(a) any material non-compliance by a member of senior management;
(b) any material non-compliance by the licensed insurer with its legal
and regulatory obligations, if the compliance function is of the
opinion that
33

(i) senior management is not taking the necessary remedial action;
and
(ii) a delay would be prejudicial to the licensed insurer or its
customers; and
(c) any material enforcement action taken by the Commission against
the licensed insurer.
Compliance procedures and controls
31. (1) A licensed insurer must establish and maintain compliance procedures
and controls that are
(a) appropriate for the nature, scale, complexity and diversity of its
business;
(b) designed to ensure compliance
(i) with its compliance policies and its legal and regulatory
obligations;
(ii) by the board, senior management and employees with its
compliance policies; and
(iii) with its internal controls;
(c) adequate to identify compliance breaches; and
(d) effectively implemented.
(2) The board must
(a) approve the compliance policy; and
(b) on at least an annual basis
(i) review the compliance policy; and
(ii) assess the effectiveness of the compliance policy and the
compliance procedures and controls in managing the
compliance risk of the licensed insurer.
Appointed actuary
32. The fact that a person is the appointed external actuary of more than one
licensed insurer is not, in itself, a conflict of interest.
Actuarial function
33. (1) The principal responsibilities of the actuarial function are the evaluation
and monitoring of, and the provision of advice to the licensed insurer concerning
(a) capital adequacy;
(b) technical provisions;
(c) premium and pricing;
(d) reinsurance; and
(e) compliance with the obligations of the licensed insurer concerning
the matters specified in paragraphs (a) to (d).
(2) The actuarial function must carry out such activities as are necessary
to undertake the responsibilities specified in subparagraph (1) and, in
34

particular, must evaluate, review, and where appropriate calculate, and provide
advice on
(a) actuarial and financial risks;
(b) the investment policies and the valuation of assets;
(c) the solvency position, including a calculation of minimum capital
resources required for regulatory purposes and liability and loss
provisions;
(d) the prospective solvency position;
(e) the risk assessment and management policies and controls relevant
to actuarial matters or to financial condition;
(f) the distribution to policyholders and beneficiaries of payments and
other benefits on participating policies;
(g) the underwriting policies;
(h) the design of the reinsurance programme in line with the risk
strategy as approved by the board, and the subsequent negotiation of
reinsurance arrangements;
(i) product development and design, including the terms and conditions
of insurance contracts;
(j) the sufficiency and quality of data used in the calculation of
technical provisions;
(k) risk modelling, where applicable;
(l) experience reviews and profit testing;
(m) the completion of a financial condition report; and
(n) any distribution or other benefits to be paid to shareholders.
(3) If the appointed actuary of a licensed insurer is an employee of the
licensed insurer, the appointed actuary must be appointed as the key person in
the actuarial function.
(4) The person appointed as the key person in the actuarial function must
report to
(a) the board on
(i) the matters specified in subparagraph (2)(a), (b) and (e); and
(ii) any matter that may have an adverse material impact on the
solvency or financial condition of the licensed insurer or its
ability to meet its liability to customers;
(iii) any circumstance that may be material to an actuarial review of
the licensed insurer, including that the technical provisions and
other liabilities are not adequate;
(iv) if the licensed insurer is in contravention of, or the actuarial
function considers that it is likely to contravene, any provisions
of the Act or the directives, concerning the matters specified in
35

subparagraph (1)(a) or (b) or any requirements concerning
solvency or financial condition;
(v) if, in the opinion of the actuarial function, the reinsurance cover
held by the licensed insurer is not adequate or the data available
to the actuarial function is insufficient, or of insufficient quality,
to enable it to carry out its functions and undertake its
responsibilities; and
(vi) on any other matter specified by the board; and
(b) to the senior management on the matters specified in subparagraph
(1)(c) and (d).
Internal audit function
34. (1) The principal responsibility of the internal audit function is to provide
the board with independent assurance of the quality and effectiveness of the
governance framework, including its risk management systems and internal
controls.
(2) The principal duties of the internal audit function are
(a) assessing whether the existing risk management strategy, policies,
procedures and controls, including internal controls remain
sufficient, effective and appropriate for the business of the licensed
insurer;
(b) assessing whether the risk management strategy, policies,
procedures and controls, including internal controls, are being
implemented and complied with;
(c) assessing whether the procedures and controls for monitoring and
assessing the on-going capital and solvency requirements are
effective and are being implemented;
(d) assessing the reliability, integrity and completeness of the
accounting, financial reporting, management information and
information technology systems;
(e) reviewing on at least an annual basis the risk management and
compliance functions; and
(f) monitoring the information systems.
(3) The responsibilities specified in subparagraph (1) must extend to all
the activities of a licensed insurer, including outsourced activities, and where
a licensed insurer has established branches or subsidiaries, to those branches
and subsidiaries.
(4) The internal audit function must be subject to independent review by
the audit committee and the external auditor.
(5) The internal audit function must
(a) be independent from management and must not, in any way, be
involved in the operation of the business of the licensed insurer; and
(b) report directly to the board, through the key person in the control
function.
36

(6) The internal audit function must be given the authority, for the
purposes of fulfilling its responsibilities, to
(a) undertake, on the internal audit function’s initiative, a review of any
department, unit or function;
(b) require management to respond to any internal audit report,
including on remediation or mitigation plans; and
(c) decline to carry out any task requested by the senior management if
the internal audit function considers that it is inconsistent with its
functions.
Internal audit reports to be submitted to Commission
35. A licensed insurer must
(a) within 21 days after the last day of each calendar quarter, provide
the Commission with a list of reports that have been prepared by the
internal audit function during that calendar quarter, with a summary
of the areas covered by each report; and
(b) on the written request of the Commission, submit to the Commission
copies of the internal reports specified in the Commission’s request,
within the time period specified in the request.
Outsourcing
Responsibility for outsourced activities
36. (1) Where a licensed insurer outsources an activity, the licensed insurer
(a) must oversee the performance of the activity by the service provider;
and
(b) remains responsible for
(i) the performance of the activity by the service provider; and
(ii) any failure by the service provider in relation to the performance
of the activity.
(2) A licensed insurer must not outsource
(a) any duties of the compliance function; or
(b) any activity if the outsourcing of that activity would
(i) impair the Commission’s ability to supervise the licensed
insurer; or
(ii) affect the rights of a customer or potential customer against the
licensed insurer, including the right to obtain legal redress.
(3) A licensed insurer must not outsource any of the duties of the risk
management function, the internal audit function or the actuarial function
without the prior written approval of the Commission.
(4) Subparagraph (2)(a) does not prevent the compliance function being
undertaken at a group level, where approved by the Commission.
(5) A control function undertaken at a group level is considered to be an
outsourced function for the purposes of subparagraph (3).
37

(6) Subparagraph (3) does not affect or limit the requirement to have an
appointed actuary.
Outsourcing of material activities
37. A licensed insurer must not enter into an outsourcing arrangement in relation
to any material activity unless
(a) the board of the licensed insurer has
(i) undertaken an assessment of the outsourcing risk;
(ii) satisfied itself as to the expertise and experience of the service
provider;
(iii) satisfied itself that the charges, fees and costs payable under the
outsourcing contracts are reasonable given the activities to be
undertaken by the service provider under the agreement and are
affordable given the current and likely future income and costs
of the licensed insurer;
(iv) taking full account of the matters specified in subparagraphs (i),
(ii) and (iii), approved the outsourcing arrangement; and
(v) satisfied itself that the outsourcing will be subject to appropriate
controls;
(b) the licensed insurer has
(i) established an outsourcing policy with respect to the activities
to be outsourced (“the relevant activities”); and
(ii) given the Commission not less than 14 days’ notice of its
intention to do so.
Outsourcing policy
38. (1) The outsourcing policy must
(a) consider the potential effects of outsourcing on the ability of the
compliance function and the internal audit function to undertake its
duties;
(b) include an evaluation of whether, and the extent to which, the
relevant activities are appropriate for outsourcing;
(c) set out the internal review and approvals required;
(d) specify criteria for making outsourcing decisions, including how,
and to whom, particular types of relevant activities should be
outsourced; and
(e) provide for outsourcing only as permitted by, and in accordance
with, this directive.
(2) The board of a licensed insurer
(a) must approve the outsourcing policy of the licensed insurer and keep
it under review; and
(b) is responsible for ensuring that any outsourcing arrangements are
put in place and operated in accordance with the outsourcing policy.
38

Managing outsourcing risks
39. (1) If a licensed insurer outsources any activities, it must establish and
maintain appropriate and adequate procedures and controls to manage its
outsourcing risk.
(2) Without limiting subparagraph (1), the outsourcing management risk
procedures and controls must
(a) provide for the monitoring and controlling of the outsourcing
arrangements of the licensed insurer; and
(b) take account of the key outsourcing risks specified in Schedule 2.
Outsourcing arrangements
40. (1) A licensed insurer must, before entering into any outsourcing
arrangement, whether material or otherwise, undertake appropriate due diligence
with respect to the service provider to whom the activities will be outsourced to
enable it to assess
(a) the service provider’s capacity and ability to undertake the
outsourced activity; and
(b) the risks associated with outsourcing the proposed activity to the
service provider.
(2) The outsourcing of any material activity must be governed by a
written contract with the service provider that
(a) clearly specifies all material aspects of the outsourcing arrangement,
including
(i) the activities to be outsourced, including agreed service and
performance levels;
(ii) the rights and responsibilities of the parties;
(iii) the protection by the service provider of confidential
information relating to the licensed insurer or its customers;
(iv) provisions for monitoring and assessing the outsourcing;
(v) provisions for the termination of the arrangement by the
licensed insurer; and
(vi) an agreed mechanism for resolving disputes;
(b) prohibits outsourcing of any activities relating to the internal audit
function and specifies the circumstances, if any, in which the service
provider may subcontract any other outsourced activities;
(c) gives the licensed insurer and its auditor access to all documents and
information relevant to the outsourced activity; and
(d) provides that the governing law of the outsourcing contract is
Ghanaian Law.
(3) A licensed insurer must establish and maintain a contingency plan
for each outsourcing agreement that it enters into.
39

Supervision of outsourced activities
41. If the Commission exercises its power under section 164(1)(b) of the Act to
inspect the business or premises of a service provider to whom a licensed insurer
has outsourced activities and the business or premises of the service provider are
situated outside Ghana, the Commission may require the licensed insurer to pay its
reasonable costs of undertaking the inspection.
Business Continuity
Business continuity plans
42. (1) The board of a licensed insurer must establish or approve a business
continuity policy, and ensure that business continuity arrangements are put in place,
aimed at ensuring that, in the event of an unforeseen interruption or disruption
(a) the licensed insurer is able to continue to carry on its insurance
business and to meet its legal and regulatory obligations;
(b) losses to the licensed insurer’s functions, systems and data are
limited and any losses may be recovered in a timely manner; and
(c) where the severity of the interruption or disruption results in the
licensed insurer ceasing its insurance business, or any part of it, it is
able to resume its business in a timely manner.
(2) The business continuity policy and arrangements must be
(a) appropriate for the nature, scale, complexity and diversity of the
business and risk profile of the licensed insurer; and
(b) regularly reviewed and tested and updated as required.
(3) Without limiting subparagraph (1) or (2), the interruptions and
disruptions covered by the business continuity plan and arrangements must
include
(a) the loss or failure of internal and external resources, including
human resources, systems and other assets;
(b) the loss or corruption of data and other information; and
(c) external events, such as criminal acts, weather events and other
natural disasters.
GUIDELINES
Control Functions
38. Section 77(1) of the Act requires a licensed insurer to establish the following
specific control functions:
(a) a risk management function;
(b) a compliance function;
(c) an actuarial function; and
(d) an internal audit function.
40

However, if the nature, scale, complexity and diversity of the business and the
risks that it faces, warrant, the licensed insurer must establish other control
functions in accordance with section 77(1)(e) of the Act.
39. The term “function” is not defined in either the Act or the directives. The
Commission considers a function to be “an individual, a group of individuals,
a department or an external service provider (if permitted) having
responsibility for the activities required to be carried out.
40. The control functions are an integral part of the risk management system and
the internal control framework. The control functions, which must operate on
a permanent and continuous basis, provide important governance checks and
balances and provide assurance to the board in the fulfilment of its oversight
role. However, this does not relieve the board or senior management of their
respective governance and related responsibilities.
41. Paragraph 20(3) of the directive requires the board to ensure that the
performance of each control function is periodically assessed. The
Commission expects the assessment to be undertaken by the internal audit
function (for control functions other than internal audit) or by an objective
and suitably qualified and experienced external assessor.
42. Section 77(2)(a) of the Act requires that each control function must be
“provided with the authority, independence and resources required to enable
it to operate effectively”. The Commission expects that the board itself will
address these requirements and document the authority and responsibilities
of each control function within the documentation that establishes and
describes the governance framework.
43. In order to comply with the requirement for independence, a control function
must
(a) be independent from senior management and other control functions,
to the extent that these are not combined; and
(b) avoid conflicts of interest.
If conflicts of interest cannot be avoided, arrangements approved by the
board must be put in place to manage them effectively.
44. Paragraph 20(1)(e) of the directive requires that a control function has the
necessary access to employees, service providers, the board and board
committees. Access must be an initiative of the key person in the control
function and include the right to conduct investigations of possible
contraventions of the Act and directives and to request assistance from
specialists both within the licensed insurer and externally.
45. In order to ensure that each control function is adequately resourced, the
person responsible for the control function must regularly review the
adequacy of the function’s resources and, if necessary, request senior
management to provide additional resources. Any significant differences
between the control function and senior management on resourcing issues
must be brought before the board or appropriate board committee by the key
person responsible for the control function, for resolution by the board.
41

46. It may be appropriate for certain control functions to be combined,
particularly in the case of a smaller licensed insurer. Paragraph 21 of the
directive sets out the basis for, and the limitations on, combining control
functions.
Key Persons in Control Functions
47. The Act defines “key person in a control function” as “an individual
appointed to undertake, or have responsibility for, and oversight of, a control
function”. An individual appointed as key person in a control function should
have an appropriate level of authority and should not have any operational
responsibilities.
48. The Commission expects that the board or relevant board committee approve
the appointment, performance assessment, remuneration, discipline and
dismissal of key persons in a control function.
49. The board must give each key person in a control function the authority and
responsibility to report to the board or a board committee periodically. The
board must set the frequency and content of the reports. The reporting should
include
(a) information as to the control function’s strategy and longer-term goals
and the progress in achieving these;
(b) annual or other periodic operational plans describing shorter term
goals and the progress in achieving these; and
(c) resources (such as personnel, budget, etc.), including an analysis on
the adequacy of these resources.
50. A licensed insurer will not be able to comply with the requirement of the Act
that each control function is independent unless the key person in the control
function is also independent from senior management. The Commission
considers that independence goes beyond mere reporting lines. A key person
in a control function must also be free of any pressure that may be applied by
senior management, including by having the ability to influence the
appointment or termination of appointment of the key person in the control
function or the remuneration of the person, or otherwise.
51. Paragraph 22(5) of the directive provides that, if control functions are
combined, the individual who was appointed as the key person in the
combined control function also serves as the key person in each of the
combined control functions. A licensed insurer is not, therefore, permitted, to
appoint different individuals to be responsible for each of the combined
control functions.
Risks to be Provided for in Risk Management System
52. A brief description of the specific risks referenced in the Act or the directive
is provided below:
Insurance risk
Insurance risk (sometimes referred to as technical risk) is defined by the IAIS
as including those risks that are directly or indirectly associated with the
42
