technical or actuarial bases of calculation for premiums and technical
provisions together with risks associated with operating expenses and
excessive or uncoordinated growth. The effect of such risks - if they
materialise - is that the company may no longer be able to meet the
guaranteed obligations fully using the funds established for this purpose,
because either the claims frequency, the claims amounts, or the expenses for
administration and settlement are higher than expected.
In determining insurance risk and pricing risk, a licensed insurer will need
to take into account any minimum premium rates prescribed by the
Commission under section 256 of the Act.
Credit risk
Credit risk is the risk that a borrower or other counterparty will fail to meet
its obligations to a licensed insurer in accordance with the agreed terms. The
management of credit risk is an important element of a comprehensive
approach to risk management and is an important factor in the long-term
success of a licensed insurer. It is therefore important that the risk
management system is capable of monitoring and assessing credit exposures.
The Commission considers that, in order to assess the credit exposures of a
licensed insurer effectively, the credit risk management strategy and polices
of a licensed insurer will need to
(a) establish limits for credit and asset exposures to counterparties and
related parties.
(b) evaluate and monitor credit exposures against pre-approved limits and
report to the board or senior management any breaches of these limits;
and
(c) provide for the reduction or cancellation of limits to a particular
counterparty where the counterparty is known to be experiencing
problems.
Liquidity risk
Liquidity risk is the risk that a licensed insurer is not able to fund its
obligations as they fall due for payment because it does not have sufficient
liquid assets to do so. The obligations may be to policyholders or other
creditors.
Given the importance of liquidity to licensed insurers, and the range of
business functions that can impact on liquidity, directors and senior
management and other relevant employees should have a thorough
understanding of liquidity risk management and, in particular, how other
risks, including credit and operational risk can impact on liquidity. The
Commission expects the risk management system to cover at least the
following
(a) the level of mismatch between expected asset and liability cash flows;
under normal and abnormal operating conditions (scenario analysis);
(b) the liquidity of assets and the level of liquid assets held by the licensed
insurer;
43

(c) policyholder claims and other liability commitments;
(d) the uncertainty of incidence, timing and magnitude of insurance
liabilities; and
(e) other sources of funding available to the licensed insurer including
reinsurance, borrowing and lines of credit.
Market risk
Market risk is the risk to the financial condition of a licensed insurer arising
from movements in the level or volatility of market prices of assets, liabilities
and financial instruments, whether on all investments as a whole (general
market risk) or on an individual investment (specific market risk). In order to
minimize market risk, the risk management strategy and policies should
clearly document the investment decision making framework including asset
allocations, liability portfolio matching criteria, and performance analysis.
It should also include information on the process for monitoring, controlling
and reporting investment activity and exposures.
Operational risk
Operational risk arises out of the way that a licensed insurer is operated and
includes most risks that result from inadequate or failed internal processes,
people and systems or from external events.
The following are examples of operational risks
(a) internal and external fraud;
(b) employment practices and workplace safety, including workers
compensation claims and breach of employee health and safety rules;
(c) products and business practices, including fiduciary breaches, misuse
of confidential customer information, money laundering, and the sale
of unauthorised products;
(d) damage to physical assets;
(e) business disruption and system failures;
(f) execution, delivery and process management, including data entry
errors, collateral management failures, incomplete legal
documentation, non-customer counterparty misperformance and
vendor disputes.
The Commission expects that licensed insurers will have in place written
documentation covering all business functions and internal processes and
contingency plans to deal with occasions on which processes fail.
Reputational risk
Reputational risk is the risk of loss of future business, and therefore revenue,
due to breaches or perceived breaches of insurance contracts, including a
failure to pay claims.
44

Legal risk
Legal risk includes, but is not limited to, exposure to fines, penalties, or
punitive damages resulting from supervisory actions, as well as private
settlements and the risk that contracts are unenforceable.
Conduct of business risk
Conduct of business is the risk to customers, licensed insurers, the insurance
sector or the insurance market that arises from licensed insurers conducting
their business in a way that does not ensure the fair treatment of customers.
This may include a number of specific risks, including basis risk, policyholder
value risk, policyholder understanding risk and mis-selling risk. The
Commission expects licensed insurers to have conduct of business rules in
place.
53. In addition, the board of a licensed insurer must consider whether any other
risks should be covered by the risk management system and paragraph 23(3)
of the directive requires, in particular, that the following risks are considered
 contagion risk.
 pricing and product design risk;
 reinsurance risk;
 outsourcing risk;
 foreign exchange risk; and
 cyber risk (which is a type of operational risk).
54. Pricing and product design risk is the risk that claims, costs or investment
returns arising from the sale of a policy are inaccurately calculated. In order
to minimize product and design risk, the risk management strategy and
policies of a licensed insurer should include policies for determining what
product lines the licensed insurer is prepared to engage in, the pricing of such
products based on the cost of, and risks associated with, the product and
prices of competing products. The risk management policies should also
cover the plans of the licensed insurer to monitor and ensure compliance with
product design and pricing policies and procedures.
55. Reinsurance risk: is the risk arising from reinsurance arrangements where
some part of individual or aggregate insurance risks is ceded to licensed
reinsurers or other licensed insurers. It is the risk that reinsurance
arrangements will be insufficient to meet the obligations to the policyholder
when the licensed insurer has relied on those arrangements to do so.
Risk Management
56. If the Commission considers that the risk management strategy, policies,
procedures and controls of a licensed insurer are not adequate to manage the
risks to which it is exposed effectively, it has the power to take enforcement
or other actions against the licensed insurer under the Act. Enforcement
actions could include the issuance of a directive requiring the licensed
insurer to strengthen its risk management process. Other actions include
requiring the licensed insurer to raise additional capital to cover the risks.
45

57. The board is ultimately responsible for the effectiveness of the risk
management strategy and policies. The Commission will look for evidence
that demonstrates that the board and senior management understand all the
risks including external risks when conducting an on-site inspection. The
Commission will also look for evidence that the board and senior
management have considered the appropriateness of the risk management
strategy and policies in the light of the licensed insurer’s risk profile and its
business plan.
58. In order to be effective, the risk management system must be understood by
all relevant employees. Relevant employees must therefore be provided with
training on the risk management systems.
Risk Management Function
59. Paragraph 25(2) of the directive provides that the risk management function
must report to the board any matter that may have an adverse material impact
on the risk management system of the licensed insurer, as soon as reasonably
practicable after it identifies the matter. However, the risk management
function must also report to the board, or the risk management committee on
all matters concerning risk management that the board, or risk management
committee, needs to be aware of to fulfil its responsibilities.
60. Paragraph 25(1) of the directive specifies that the principal duties of the risk
management function are to
(a) assist the licensed insurer to identify, assess, monitor, manage and
report on its key risks in a timely manner; and
(b) promote and sustain a sound risk culture within the licensed insurer.
Other duties include
(i) identifying the risks that the licensed insurer faces;
(ii) providing the board, the risk management committee and senior
management with risk analysis and reviews;
(iii) assisting the licensed insurer in the management of its risk;
(iv) conducting regular stress tests and scenario analyses;
(v) providing the board, or the risk management committee, if
appropriate, with written reports on material adverse changes in
the risk profile of the licensed insurer;
(vi) conducting regular assessments of the risk management system
and function and monitoring the implementation of any
improvements required.
Internal Controls
61. The purpose of the internal controls established by a licensed insurer is to
assist the board and senior management to fulfil their responsibilities for the
oversight and management of the licensed insurer.
62. The Commission understands that the businesses and circumstances of each
licensed insurer are different. Subject to the paragraph above, in seeking to
46

ensure that the internal controls comply with the directive, the board and
senior management will need to exercise their judgment in determining the
scope and nature of the controls that are necessary, taking into account their
cost effectiveness.
63. The Commission expects the board to
(a) conduct periodic discussions with senior management concerning the
effectiveness of the internal control system;
(b) undertake a timely review of evaluations of internal controls made by
senior management and the licensed insurer’s external auditors and
internal auditors;
(c) make periodic efforts to ensure that management has promptly followed
up on recommendations and concerns expressed by its external and
internal auditors and the Commission on internal control weaknesses;
and
(d) undertake a periodic review of the appropriateness of the risk strategy
and limits.
64. The directive requires the board to approve an appropriate organisational
structure for the licensed insurer. In approving the organisational structure,
the Commission expects the board to take account of the general
requirements with respect to the corporate governance framework set out in
the directive. In determining whether the organisational structure of a
licensed insurer is appropriate, the Commission will need to be satisfied that
it
(a) enables appropriate delegation of authority and responsibility and
segregation of duties; and
(b) promotes the effective and prudent management of the licensed insurer
and the board’s oversight of that management.
65. The directive provides that the senior management of a licensed insurer has
responsibility for implementing the strategies and policies approved by the
board and for ensuring that the required internal controls are established and
maintained. The Commission understands that, where appropriate, senior
management will delegate specific responsibilities to other suitably qualified
or experienced staff. However, senior management must retain an oversight
role.
66. In order to ensure that the internal controls are effective, it is important for
the board and senior management to promote a culture within the licensed
insurer that emphasises and demonstrates to all levels of personnel the
importance of internal controls. All members of staff must understand their
role in the internal controls process and be fully engaged in the process. The
board and senior management should also promote high ethical and integrity
standards within the licensed insurer.
47

Appointed Actuary
67. Section 79 of the Act set out requirements in respect of potential conflicts of
interest when an external actuary is to be, or has been, appointed as the
appointed actuary.
68. The existence and extent of a conflict of interest can be difficult to identify.
The following are examples of circumstances that the Commission consider
may give rise to a conflict of interest:
(a) The external actuary acts for another licensed insurer in circumstances
where the actuary may become aware of commercially sensitive
information, or the actuary provides advice that may harm the other
client (such as a new product which has the potential to reduce the
market share of the actuary’s other client).
(b) The external actuary has a direct or indirect interest in another licensed
insurer.
(c) The external actuary has a direct or indirect interest in the licensed
insurer for which he or she acts or proposes to act.
(d) The remuneration of an external actuary (for example in relation to
work on a new product) is linked, or partially linked, to the success of
the new product or to the performance of the licensed insurer.
(e) The licensed insurer provides the external actuary with instructions
which are not compatible with the actuary’s professional duties or
obligations.
(f) The external actuary sits on a disciplinary body that is reviewing, or
has recently reviewed, a complaint against the actuary of another
licensed insurer, as the licensed insurer is likely to have had access to
confidential information.
69. It is probable that the actuarial institute, association or body of which the
external actuary is a member will have published standards and guidance on
conflicts of interest and their management. This may assist the board to
decide whether the conflict can be managed and, if so, how.
Actuarial Function
70. The Commission does not expect the key person in the actuarial function to
be a fully qualified actuary. However, the Commission is unlikely to approve
a person for appointment unless the person satisfies its guidelines for
appointment.
Internal Audit Function
71. The internal audit function provides an independent assessment of the
adequacy of, and compliance with, the established strategy, policies
procedures and controls. The internal audit function must be independent
from the day-to-day functioning of the licensed insurer, including the day-to-
day operation of its internal controls, and must have access to all activities
conducted by the licensed insurer, including at its branches and any
subsidiaries.
48

72. In order to undertake its duties effectively, the scope of the internal audit
should usually include:
(a) establishing and implementing a risk-based audit plan;
(b) reviewing and evaluating the adequacy and effectiveness of the policies
and procedures;
(c) reviewing levels of compliance;
(d) reviewing management and financial information systems;
(e) reviewing the accuracy and reliability of the accounting records and
financial reports;
(f) reviewing and evaluating the means of safeguarding the assets of the
licensed insurer and of policyholders;
(g) an appraisal of the economy and efficiency of the operations;
(h) a review of the systems established to ensure compliance with the
regulatory obligations of the licensed insurer; and
(i) testing the reliability and timeliness of the regulatory reporting.
The internal audit function should conduct special investigations, as
appropriate.
73. Although the internal audit function and the licensed insurer’s external
auditors have different roles, it will be useful for the two to coordinate to
ensure that both are operating as efficiently and effectively as possible and
that the internal audit function is providing maximum value.
Outsourcing
74. Although outsourcing may have benefits, it also exposes a licensed insurer to
additional risks as outsourcing may transfer risk, management and
compliance to service providers who are not regulated by the Commission or
any other regulator. The risks are potentially greater when the service
provider is located outside Ghana. An over-reliance on service providers may
also impact on the ability of a licensed insurer to manage its risk or on its
control and oversight of the functions that it has outsourced.
75. The requirements in the directive and these Guidelines draw on the
requirements of the ICPs supplemented by the Joint Forum Paper
“Outsourcing in Financial Services” published in February 2005. The Joint
Forum comprises representatives of the Basel Committee on Banking
Supervision, the International Association of Insurance Supervisors and the
International Organization of Securities Commissions.
76. Outsourcing covers all activities that a licensed insurer would otherwise
normally have undertaken itself, not just those activities that are regulated
under the Insurance Act as the performance of some activities, even though
not regulated, may have a significant impact on the regulatory obligations of
a licensed insurer.
77. The Joint Forum identify the following key outsourcing risks which should be
borne in mind by the directors and senior management of a licensed insurer
49

when developing and implementing its outsourcing policy and its outsourcing
systems and controls:
Strategic Risk:
(a) The service provider may conduct activities on its own behalf which are
inconsistent with the overall strategic goals of the licensed insurer.
(b) Failure to implement appropriate oversight of the outsource provider.
(c) Inadequate expertise to oversee the service provider.
Reputation Risk:
Poor service from the service provider.
(a) Customer interaction is not consistent with overall standards of the
licensed insurer.
(b) Practices not in line with stated practices (ethical or otherwise) of the
licensed insurer.
Compliance Risk:
(a) Failure to comply with legal and regulatory obligations of the licensed
insurer.
(b) Service provider has inadequate compliance systems and controls.
Operational Risk:
(a) Technology failure.
(b) Inadequate financial capacity to fulfil obligations and/or provide
remedies.
(c) Fraud or error.
Cyber risk:
Risk that firms find it difficult/costly to monitor outsourcing performance.
Exit Strategy Risk:
(a) The risk that appropriate exit strategies are not in place which could
arise from over-reliance on one service provider, the loss of relevant
skills in the licensed insurer itself preventing it bringing the activity
back in-house, and contracts which make a speedy exit prohibitively
expensive.
(b) Limited ability to return services to home country due to lack of staff or
loss of intellectual history.
Counterparty Risk:
(a) Inappropriate underwriting or credit assessments.
(b) Quality of receivables may diminish.
50

Country Risk:
(a) Political, social and legal climate may create added risk.
(b) Business continuity planning is more complex.
Contractual Risk:
Ability to enforce contract.
Access Risk
(a) Outsourcing arrangement hinders ability of the licensed insurer to
provide timely data and other information to the Commission.
(b) Additional layer of difficulty in regulator understanding activities of the
service provider.
Concentration and Systemic Risk
(a) Overall industry has significant exposure to outsource provider.
(b) Concentration risk has a number of facets, including:
(i) Lack of control of individual firms over provider; and
(ii) Systemic risk to insurance sector, or wider financial sector.
78. Paragraph 36(2)(b)(i) of the directive prohibits the outsourcing of an activity
if the outsourcing of that activity would impair the Commission’s ability to
supervise the licensed insurer. The Commission considers, for example, that
its ability to supervise a licensed insurer would be impaired if an activity was
outsourced that the Commission would wish to inspect on an on-site
inspection to a service provider in circumstances where the performance of
the activity cannot be fully and readily assessed by the Commission.
79. Paragraph 37 of the directive sets out restrictions on the outsourcing of
material activities. Materiality will depend upon the individual circumstances
of the licensed insurer. However, the following factors should be taken into
account:
(a) whether the activity is of such importance that any weakness or failure
in the provision of the activity could have a significant effect on the
ability of the licensed insurer to meet its regulatory obligations or to
continue in business;
(b) whether the activities are important to the payment of claims or the
servicing of customers;
(c) whether the activity has a significant impact on risk management.
80. Paragraph 37(a)(iii) of the directive provides that the board must satisfy itself
that the charges, fees and costs payable under the outsourcing contracts are
reasonable given the activities to be undertaken by the service provider under
the agreement and are affordable given the current and likely future income
and costs of the licensed insurer. In the case where the service provider is an
associate company of the licensed insurer, the Commission will need to be
satisfied that the outsourcing arrangements are not being used as a
51

mechanism for effecting intra-group transfers beyond the real value of the
services provided.
81. Paragraph 38(2) of the directive provides that the outsourcing contract must
clearly set out all material aspects of the outsourcing arrangements. What is
material will depend, in part, to the circumstances and the activities to be
outsourced. However, in addition to the matters specified in the paragraph,
the Commission expects that the following would usually be “material”:
(a) the ownership of intellectual property after termination;
(b) the transfer of documents and information back to the licensed insurer
after termination;
(c) provisions providing for the possible insolvency of the service provider;
(d) if the service provider is located outside Ghana, choice of law
provisions and provisions specifying how disputes are to be dealt with,
e.g., arbitration and mediation clauses and, in the event that a dispute
is subject to court proceedings at the instance of any party, the court
that the parties agree must have jurisdiction to determine the dispute;
(e) whether the service provider can subcontract any of its responsibilities
and, if so, the extent to which it may do so and the conditions applicable
to sub-contracting arrangements.
82. Where the service provider is entitled to subcontract its responsibilities, it is
important that the licensed insurer’s risk management systems and controls
are not compromised. The licensed insurer should therefore be aware of any
subcontracting arrangements and the service provider should normally be
required to seek the consent of the licensed insurer before entering into a
subcontract arrangement with respect to the outsourced activities.
Business Continuity
83. Paragraph 42 of the directive requires a licensed insurer to put in place an
appropriate business continuity policy and business continuity arrangements.
This will usually require an assessment to determine reasonable measures
that can be taken to reduce the likelihood of a disruption and the impact of a
disruption, should it take place. The Commission considers that an
assessment should cover, at least:
(a) the types of disruptions that may occur, including short-term, medium-
term and long-term;
(b) the probability of each type of disruption occurring (taking into account
any particular vulnerabilities or susceptibilities of the licensed insurer
and its business);
(c) the probable impact of each type of disruption, and the worst-case
scenario; and
(d) the likely timescale of the various types of disruption.
84. The impact of a disruption, should it take place, can be reduced by
contingency arrangements, for example by ensuring that replacement human
and other resources are available if required (whether through outsourcing
or otherwise).
52

85. The business continuity policy and arrangements should be documented, and
available for the Commission to review, if required. The policy should
include:
(a) a formal business continuity plan that sets out the arrangements made
to reduce the impact of disruptions, including resource requirements
and the arrangements for obtaining these resources, the recovery
priorities for the licensed insurer’s business and operations and
arrangements for communicating internally and externally, including
to the Commission and customers;
(b) escalation and invocation plans that outline the procedures for
implementing the business continuity plans, with relevant contact
information;
(c) procedures for validating the integrity of data and other information
affected by the disruption; and
(d) the arrangements put in place to review, test and update the
contingency plan and arrangements.
PART 3 – REINSURANCE
Preliminary
Interpretation for this Part
43. (1) In this Part, unless stated otherwise and with appropriate modifications,
a reference to
(a) “ceded reinsurance” shall be taken to include a reference to ceded
retrocession;
(b) a “ceding insurer” shall be taken to include a reference to a ceding
reinsurer;
(c) a “reinsurer” shall be taken to include a reference to a
retrocessionaire; and
(d) a reinsurance strategy, procedures or programme shall be taken to
include a reference to a retrocession strategy, procedures or
programme.
(2) Paragraph 59 applies to a foreign reinsurer that maintains a contact office in
Ghana.
Qualifying foreign reinsurer
44. (1) A foreign reinsurer is a “qualifying foreign reinsurer’ if the foreign
reinsurer has a
(a) a financial strength rating of
(i) A+, A, B+, B or C+ assigned to it by the A. M. Best Company;
(ii) AAA, AA, A, BBB or BB assigned to it by the Fitch Group or
Standard & Poors; or
(iii) Aaa, Aa, A or Baa assigned to it by Moody’s Corporation;
53

(iv) AAA, AA, A, BBB or BB assigned to it by Global Credit Rating
(GCR); and
(b) such other financial strength rating as may be approved by the
Commission on application by a licensed insurer.
(2) If a foreign reinsurer has been rated by two or more of the above rating
agencies, the most recent rating shall be used to determine whether the foreign
reinsurer is a qualifying reinsurer.
Reinsurance strategy, procedures and programme
Reinsurance strategy
45. (1) The reinsurance strategy of a licensed insurer, established and
maintained under section 72(1)(a) of the Act must form a part of its overall risk
management and capital management strategies.
(2) The reinsurance strategy must set out
(a) the objectives of the insurer for using reinsurance; and
(b) risk concentration levels and ceding limits, which must take full
account of the insurer’s risk appetite;
(c) the mechanisms to manage and control reinsurance risks; and
(d) a methodology for determining the insurer’s reinsurance
programme, including
(i) the reinsurance to be purchased;
(ii) the setting of net retention limits;
(iii) the selection of reinsurers;
(iv) the assessment of the security of reinsurers and the collateral, if
any, required; and
(v) monitoring of the reinsurance arrangements, including
appropriate reporting and control systems.
(3) The reinsurance strategy of a licensed insurer shall
(a) identify its tolerance to risk;
(b) determine its risk appetite, including the determination of gross and
net retention limits;
(c) specify how the types of reinsurance arrangements most appropriate
to manage and limit the risks to its level of risk tolerance are to be
determined;
(d) specify the insurer’s appetite for credit risk and how credit risk is to
be managed, including by
(i) setting limits on risks ceded to individual reinsurers; and
(ii) ensuring an adequate spread of risk between reinsurers;
(e) specify how liquidity risk arising from a timing mismatch between
the payment of claims and the receipt of reinsurance recoveries is to
be managed; and
54

(f) provide for the determination of whether reinsurance brokers and
other intermediaries should be employed and, if so, their role and
how they are to be selected, monitored and managed.
(4) The reinsurance strategy shall take into account
(a) the structure of the reinsurance arrangements, including any
alternative risk transfer arrangements that may be in place;
(b) the extent to which relevant functions are outsourced; and
(c) the extent of any credit risk mitigation in place.
Reinsurance procedures
46. (1) The reinsurance procedures of a licensed insurer, established and
maintained under section 72(1)(b) of the Act must include
(a) procedures and criteria for the selection of reinsurers, taking into
account
(i) appropriate levels of aggregate exposure to a single reinsurer or
different reinsurers in the same group;
(ii) the credit risks associated with the reinsurers;
(b) limits on the amount and type of insurance that will be automatically
covered by reinsurance treaties;
(c) criteria for purchasing facultative reinsurance;
(d) procedures that provide for
(i) timely payments of reinsurance premiums to reinsurers; and
(ii) timely collections of reinsurance recoveries.
(2) The reinsurance procedures shall require that any deviation from the
reinsurance strategy must have the prior documented approval of the board.
Reinsurance programme
47. (1) The reinsurance programme set or approved by a licensed insurer in
accordance with section 72(2) of the Act comprises the detailed implementation of
the reinsurance strategy.
(2) The reinsurance programme must be consistent with the reinsurance
strategy and, with respect to the financial year it covers
(a) identify the risk retention levels appropriate for its tolerance to risk,
by class of business and for its business taken as a whole, including
setting
(i) limits on net retention levels for the year;
(ii) the proportion of business to be ceded in the financial year, with
the objective that net retentions are commensurate with its
financial resources; and
(b) specify
(i) the reinsurance to be purchased by the insurer in the financial
year; and
55

(ii) whether collateral is to be required from any reinsurer and, if so,
the amount and type of collateral required.
Internal controls
48. The internal controls of a licensed insurer shall be designed to ensure that
(a) the reinsurance provided for in the reinsurance programme is in
place at all times;
(b) the terms of reinsurance contracts entered into are in accordance
with the reinsurance strategy and reinsurance programme;
(c) claims under reinsurance contracts entered into by the insurer, as
cedant, are reported to the reinsurer in a timely fashion and in
accordance with the reinsurance contract;
(d) reinsurance claims payments are promptly collected; and
(e) any failure to comply with subparagraphs (a) to (e) is identified and
immediately reported to senior management and the board.
Responsibilities of board and senior management with respect to reinsurance
49. (1) The board of a licensed insurer is responsible for
(a) setting, or approving, the reinsurance strategy;
(b) the oversight and monitoring of the implementation of the
reinsurance strategy by senior management, and its effectiveness;
and
(c) periodically reviewing the reinsurance strategy and, whenever there
have been material changes to the business, underwriting strategy
or circumstances of the insurer.
(2) The senior management of a licensed insurer is responsible for
(a) setting clear, documented reinsurance procedures that comply with
paragraph 46;
(b) developing the reinsurance programme; and
(c) regularly reviewing the performance of the reinsurance
arrangements to ensure that they are functioning as intended and
reporting to the board on any deficiencies.
Submission of reinsurance programme to the Commission
50. (1) A licensed insurer shall submit a draft of its reinsurance programme for
a financial year to the Commission for its approval on or before 15 November of
the previous year.
(2) Without limiting paragraph 47, the draft reinsurance programme
must specify
(a) each reinsurance treaty that the insurer intends to purchase;
(b) the principal terms and conditions that it intends to negotiate for
each treaty;
(c) any facultative reinsurance contracts that it intends to enter into, as
cedant, with foreign insurers or reinsurers;
56

(d) details of any security that it intends to take on any insurance treaty;
(e) details of any reinsurance intermediaries involved, whether acting
for the insurer or the reinsurer.
(3) The draft reinsurance programme must be accompanied by evidence
of payment of the insurer’s treaty balances for the current financial year, up to
30 June of that year.
(4) A licensed insurer shall not enter into any reinsurance contract prior
to receiving the Commission’s approval of the draft programme.
(5) A licensed insurer shall submit its completed treaty programme to
the Commission for a financial year, together with the premiums paid to
reinsurers during that year, on or before 15 December of that year.
(6) A licensed insurer shall notify the Commission in writing if it makes
any material changes to its reinsurance programme within fourteen days of
making the change.
GUIDELINES
Objectives of reinsurance
86. Reinsurance is usually considered to serve the following functions, not all of
which will apply to all insurers:
(a) by reducing the risk of a licensed insurer, reinsurance acts as a
substitute for capital. In essence, the insurer is able to rely on the
reinsurer’s capital. This provides a licensed insurer with additional
capacity and flexibility, enabling it, for example, to expand into new
lines of business and increase its exposure to existing business within a
short period of time.
(b) well designed reinsurance arrangements should provide stability by
limiting wide fluctuations in underwriting results. As a consequence,
the limited risk spread will allow the insurers to reduce the required
amount of their own funds at risk and hence improve the insurer’s
solvency position.
(c) reinsurance provides protection against the potential large
accumulations of individual losses that can result from catastrophic
events.
(d) reinsurers can supply technical, underwriting, pricing and claims
assistance to insurers in specialised areas where the insurer may have
little or no experience.
87. As reinsurance is a contract of indemnity, the insurer retains legal liability
for claims under the insurance contract. Therefore, although reinsurance
transfers insurance risk to the reinsurer, it creates other risks such as credit
risk, liquidity risk, operational risk and basis risk (i.e., that there is a
mismatch between the insurer’s liability under the insurance contract and the
reinsurance payment intended to cover that risk).
57

Interpretation for Part 3
88. As provided in paragraph 2, the directive applies to licensed insurers and
licensed reinsurers, unless provided otherwise. To avoid unnecessary
duplication, to simplify the drafting and to make the directive more user
friendly, the word “insurer” is taken to also include a reinsurer (unless the
directive states otherwise). Therefore, an obligation imposed on a licensed
insurer is also imposed on a licensed reinsurer. However, when the reference
is to a licensed reinsurer, the terms set out in paragraph 2 of the directive
bear the equivalent meaning for a reinsurer. See paragraph 2.
Qualifying foreign reinsurer
89. Section 73 of the Act imposes restrictions on the placement of reinsurance by
licensed insurers. Placing reinsurance with a qualifying foreign reinsurer is
permitted by section 73(1)(c) of the Act.
90. The Act (section 259) defines a “foreign reinsurer” as:
“a reinsurer that is incorporated or constituted in a jurisdiction outside the
country:
(a) the primary business of which is the business of entering into
reinsurance contracts, as reinsurer; and
(b) which does not carry on a significant amount of direct insurance
business as a percentage of the premium income of that reinsurer;”.
91. A “qualifying foreign reinsurer” is defined as a foreign reinsurer that meets
the requirements specified in the directives. Paragraph 44 of the directive
specifies those requirements. These requirements are directed towards
ensuring that the reinsurer has an adequate financial strength rating,
provided by one of the large and internationally recognized rating agencies.
The Commission’s supervisory functions
92. In order to fulfil its supervisory functions, the Commission needs to gain an
adequate understanding of, and level of comfort with (at a minimum):
(a) the reinsurance strategy and arrangements of each insurer;
(b) the procedures of each insurer for implementing the reinsurance
strategy and executing the reinsurance arrangements and the internal
controls insofar as they relate to reinsurance;
(c) the impact of reinsurance on the liquidity management of a ceding
insurer;
(d) the economic impact of the risk transfer arising out of the insurer’s
reinsurance programme; and
(e) the overall effectiveness of the reinsurance arrangements of each
insurer.
Reinsurance strategy and procedures
93. Section 72(1) of the Act requires every insurer to establish and maintain a
written reinsurance strategy. The reinsurance strategy, which as provided in
58

paragraph 45(1) of the directive is part of the underwriting and overall risk
management strategy, is a high-level document intended to set out the
insurer’s strategic objectives for reinsurance and to define the insurer’s
strategy for reinsurance management.
94. Paragraph 46 of the directive requires a licensed insurer to establish and
maintain reinsurance procedures that provide for the implementation of the
reinsurance strategy. It is senior management that has primary responsibility
for setting the reinsurance procedures.
95. The board is responsible for periodically reviewing the reinsurance strategy.
The Commission expects the board to undertake a review at least annually.
An annual review is the minimum requirement. As envisaged by paragraph
49(1)(c) of the directive, the board should also review the reinsurance
strategy when there have been material changes to its business, underwriting
strategy or circumstances. A change of circumstances would include material
changes to the status of reinsurers.
Facultative reinsurance
96. A licensed insurer may write an insurance policy that is not typical of the
business that it normally writes. This may be because the risk is a “one off”
risk or alternatively the sum insured greatly exceeds what the insurer
normally accepts. If the insurer wants or needs to cede some part of the risk
to a reinsurer, it is very likely that the risk will not fit within the normal
reinsurance arrangements such as stop loss, quota share or excess of loss, all
of which cover a book of similar risks. The insurer will need to enter into a
"one off" arrangement known as facultative reinsurance with the
reinsurer. Under facultative reinsurance, the reinsurer assesses and prices
individually the risk it is being asked to accept and enters into a separate
contract with the insurer. If the reinsurer accepts the risk, the insurer pays a
reinsurance premium to the reinsurer in the same way that it does with treaty
reinsurance.
97. Paragraph 46(1)(c) of the directive requires that the reinsurance procedures
include criteria for purchasing facultative reinsurance. A licensed insurer
must have a specific process in place to approve, monitor and confirm the
placement of each facultative risk. The Commission considers that facultative
reinsurance should usually be secured before the cedant accepts a risk that
exceeds its treaty capacity or its risk appetite.
Reinsurance programme
98. The reinsurance programme is set annually. It is intended to specify in a
reasonably detailed manner how the reinsurance strategy will be
implemented in the year to which it relates. The reinsurance programme
should set out comprehensive reinsurance arrangements for the year. The
draft reinsurance programme must be delivered to the Commission by 15
November of the previous year. This is intended to enable the Commission to
consider the draft and discuss it with the insurer so that the final reinsurance
programme, once submitted, is in a form that the Commission has no
objection to.
59

99. The Commission expects insurers to consider developing a list of pre-
approved reinsurers. However, recognising that this will not necessarily be
appropriate for all insurers, this is not a requirement.
Internal controls
100. Paragraph 48 is intended to supplement, and not replace, the general
requirements relating to internal controls.
Obligations and Restrictions
Exhaustion of local reinsurance capacity
51. (1) A licensed direct insurer must not, without the written approval of the
Commission, enter into a reinsurance contract with a foreign reinsurer unless it is
satisfied that local reinsurance capacity has been exhausted.
(2) In making a determination as to whether local reinsurance capacity
has been exhausted for the purposes of subparagraph (1), a licensed direct
insurer
(a) is required to consider the reinsurance capacity of licensed
reinsurers;
(b) is not required to consider the capacity of any other licensed direct
insurer or licensed direct insurers to accept the insurance risk
through a facultative reinsurance contract; and
(c) must take into account the most recent guidelines concerning the
determination of local reinsurance capacity issued by the
Commission.
(3) Subparagraph (2)(b) does not prevent a licensed direct insurer
entering into a facultative reinsurance contract, as cedant, with another
licensed direct insurer in accordance with paragraph 54.
Reinsurance contracts with foreign reinsurers
52. A licensed insurer must not, without the written approval of the
Commission, enter into a reinsurance contract with a foreign reinsurer that includes
the reinsurance of any of the following classes or types of insurance business
(a) motor insurance;
(b) worker’s compensation insurance;
(c) goods in transit;
(d) life insurance
(e) fidelity guarantee
Lloyd’s underwriters
53. (1) For the purposes of section 73 of the Act, and in particular section
73(1)(d) of the Act, the following are regarded as foreign reinsurers
(a) a Loyd’s underwriter or a syndicate of Lloyd’s underwriters;
(b) underwriters that are members of a recognised association of
underwriters approved by the Commission.
60

(2) For the purposes of determing compliance with paragraph 44, regard
shall be had of the financial strength rating assigned to Lloyd’s on a market
basis.
Facultative reinsurance contracts
54. (1) A licensed direct insurer must not, without the written approval of the
Commission, enter into a facultative reinsurance contract, as cedant, with a foreign
direct insurer or a foreign reinsurer otherwise than in accordance with its
reinsurance program submitted to, and approved by, the Commission under
paragraph 50.
(2) A licensed direct insurer (the ceding insurer) may only enter into a
facultative reinsurance contract with another licensed direct insurer (the
accepting insurer) if the ceding insurer
(a) is satisfied that
(i) local reinsurance capacity is exhausted;
(ii) entering into the facultative reinsurance contract is consistent
with its reinsurance, risk management and capital management
strategies;
(iii) the accepting insurer has the capacity to accept the risk;
(iv) that placing the risk with the accepting insurer will not result in
a undue concentration of risk, whether within Ghana or with the
accepting insurer; and
(b) has considered whether placing the risk should be contingent on the
accepting insurer providing security to the ceding insurer and, if so,
the ceding insurer has obtained the security.
Inwards facultative reinsurance, foreign direct insurers
55. (1) A licensed direct insurer must not, without the written approval of the
Commission
(a) enter into a facultative reinsurance contract, as accepting insurer,
with a foreign direct insurer without the written approval of the
Commission;
(b) enter into a contract with or pay any commission or remuneration to
a foreign insurance intermediary with respect to a facultative
reinsurance contract referred to in subparagraph (a).
(2) Subparagraph (1)(b) does not prevent the payment of commission or
remuneration to a foreign insurance intermediary through a licensed insurance
broker or reinsurance broker.
Fronting arrangements
56. (1) A fronting arrangement is an arrangement through which an insurer cedes
to another direct insurer or reinsurer (whether or not licensed under the Act), the
entire risk, or a significant portion of the risk, under an insurance contract that it
has entered into, while remaining liable under the insurance contract to the insured.
(2) A licensed insurer must not
61

(a) enter into a fronting arrangement with a reinsurer unless the fronting
arrangement complies with the requirements of the Act and the
directives on reinsurance; or
(b) enter into any fronting arrangement with a direct insurer.
Insurance pools and reinsurance pools
57. (1) An association of insurers is an insurance pool within the meaning of
section 259 of the Act if, in addition to sharing the insurance risk, the participating
insurers share, in pre-agreed proportions
(a) the premiums;
(b) expenses
(c) losses; and
(d) profits.
(2) An insurance pool may
(a) be established by the participating insurers acting directly as a group
or through one or more third parties, including insurance
intermediaries authorised by the participating insurers for the
purpose; or
(b) operate through a separate entity established for the purpose.
(3) A reinsurance pool is an association between two or more reinsurers
which, if they were insurers, would be an insurance pool.
(4) A licensed insurer shall not participate in an insurance pool without
the prior written approval of the Commission.
Alternative risk transfer arrangements
58. (1) An alternative risk transfer arrangement is any form of risk transfer of
insurance liabilities by an insurer, other than through a traditional reinsurance
agreement, including but not limited to
(a) securitisation of insurance risks, including through insurance-linked
securities;
(b) catastrophe bonds;
(c) reinsurance sidecars;
(d) industry loss warranties; and
(e) finite reinsurance;
(2) A licensed insurer shall not enter into a contract or arrangement that
constitutes an alternative risk transfer arrangement without the prior written
approval of the Commission.
(3) Subject to a written approval under subparagraph (2), a licensed
insurer shall not enter into any arrangement that constitutes a direct transfer of
the risk under any insurance contract entered into by the insurer, to the capital
markets.
Contact office maintained by foreign reinsurer
59. (1) A foreign reinsurer that maintains a contact office in Ghana must
62

(a) deposit the sum of USD500,000 in an account established and
maintained with a bank that is licensed by the Bank of Ghana and
approved by the Commission as an escrow agent to hold a deposit
on behalf of a foreign reinsurer;
(b) establish and maintain a separate account with a bank specified in
subparagraph (a) into which all remittances relating to the foreign
resinurer’s office in Ghana are paid; and
(c) provide the Commission with an irrevocable authority to obtain
from the bank such information concerning the account, and the
transactions into and out of the account, as the Commission may
require.
(2) A foreign reinsurer must
(a) ensure that throughout the period during which it maintains a contact
office, it is registered with the Registrar General’s Department as an
external company carrying on business in Ghana;
(b) ensure that its contact office is adequately staffed by employees who
are citizens of Ghana;
(c) submit to the Commission such periodic returns as the Commission
may require;
(d) comply with such directives and conditions as the Commission may
specify;
(e) ensure that it complies with the Commission’s directives concerning
governance and risk management, as far as appropriate to the
operation of a contact office; and
(f) the office is maintained solely as a contact office.
(3) A foreign reinsurer shall pay such annual and periodic fees to the
Commission as the Commission directs.
(4) The requirements specified under subparagraphs (1) to (3) are
conditions of the Commission’s approval.
GUIDELINES
Exhaustion of Local Reinsurance Capacity
101. ICP 13 (Reinsurance) indicates that the main consideration with respect to
the reinsurance program of a direct insurer should be whether the insurer is
adequately managing its capital and risks, particularly its underwriting risk.
On the other hand, section 4(e)(ii) of the Act requires the Commission, in
implementing its objects, to have regard for promoting growth and
development in the Ghana insurance market.
102. There is a clear tension between the two. A licensed insurer may consider that
to effectively manage its capital and risks, it needs to reinsure into the
international reinsurance market. Critical to this is the question of
geographical diversification. ICP 13.02 states:
63

“Geographical diversification ……. is a key element of ceding insurer’s
and reinsurer´s capital and risk management. Geographical
diversification can also have an impact in the jurisdiction of the ceding
insurer, in particular jurisdictions exposed to catastrophes. By ceding
insurance risk across borders, ceding insurers in the jurisdiction, and
the jurisdiction as a whole, can benefit from a reduced concentration
of insurance risk exposures at the ceding insurer and jurisdiction level
respectively. This may also contribute to the financial stability of the
jurisdiction.”
103. Therefore, even if licensed reinsurers have the capacity to take risk, requiring
a licensed insurer to reinsure with a licensed reinsurer deprives the ceding
insurer of a key element of its capital and risk management. This is even more
important when considering catastrophe or other correlated risk, including
mega risks associated with, for example, the oil and gas sectors. Although a
Ghana reinsurer may retrocede risk to the international reinsurance market,
the ceding insurer has no control over that decision. Furthermore, reinsuring
and retroceding adds a layer of transaction cost which, arguably, is not in
the best interests of policyholders as this will result in higher premiums.
104. Over the last few years, the Commission has assessed market capacity not
just against the capacity of Ghana licensed reinsurers, but against the
capacity of the market taken as a whole. In the circumstances, licensed
insurers have, in effect, been required to enter into facultative reinsurance
contracts with other direct insurers if there is insufficient reinsurance
capacity. However, there is no equivalence from a capital and risk
management perspective between a reinsurer (Ghanian or
international/regional) and a licensed insurer. Reinsuring through a
facultative contract with a local insurer will result in an increased credit risk.
105. Although licensed reinsurers are licensed, regulated and approved as
reinsurers, licensed direct insurers are not. The Commission therefore
considers that it is no longer appropriate for it to regard market capacity and
risk within the Ghana market as homogeneous. This approach does not permit
a licensed insurer to consider its own risk management requirements and,
perhaps more important, takes no account of the need and for, and the
benefits of, geographical diversification of risk. Even if the local market
(taken as a whole) has the capacity to retain all oil and gas risk, it is not
necessarily sensible for all risk to be retained in Ghana.
106. Therefore, in seeking to balance the requirements of ICP 13, its objects
(section 2 of the Act) and the Guiding Principles in section 4 of the Act, the
Commission considers that:
(a) Licensed direct insurers should be required to consider local
reinsurance capacity, i.e., the capacity of Ghana licensed reinsurers
and the default position should be that, if Ghana reinsurers have
capacity, licensed insurers should be required to reinsure, on either a
treaty or facultative basis, with one or more licensed reinsurers.
(b) Direct insurers should no longer be required to reinsure through
facultative reinsurance contracts with licensed direct insurers,
although they should be permitted to continue to do so.
64

(c) As indicated in paragraph (a), the default position should be to exhaust
local reinsurance capacity before reinsuring onto the international
market.
107. Although the exhaustion of local reinsurance capacity is the default position,
paragraph 51(1) of the directive enables direct insurers to apply to the
Commission for approval to reinsure directly into the international
reinsurance market. The Commission would only consider granting approval
if adequate justification is provided for doing so. The Commission would
consider issues such as geographical diversification and the terms of the
reinsurance cover available in the local market versus the international
market as relevant.
108. Although licensed direct insurers will still be able to cede insurance risk to
other licensed direct insurers through facultative reinsurance contracts, this
is subject to certain. Conditions. A ceding insurer must be satisfied that local
reinsurance capacity is exhausted but also that:
(a) entering into the facultative reinsurance contract is consistent with its
reinsurance, risk management and capital management strategies;
(b) the accepting insurer has the capacity to take the risk; and
(c) that placing the risk with the accepting insurer will not result in an
undue concentration of risk, whether within Ghana or with the
accepting insurer.
The ceding insurer must also have considered whether placing the risk should
be contingent on the accepting insurer providing security to the ceding
insurer and, if so, the ceding insurer has obtained the security.
The effect of this is to elevate the importance of risk and capital management
in the decision as to whether to enter into a facultative reinsurance contract.
Fronting
109. The term “fronting” is used to describe an arrangement under which a
licensed insurer (the fronting insurer) transfers all or a substantial part of the
risk under an insurance policy that it has issued to a reinsurer or another
direct insurer (usually outside the country where the fronting insurer is
located). The fronting insurer typically receives commission on the premium.
The term has a slightly modified meaning in the context of captive insurance,
but that is not relevant for the Ghana insurance market.
110. Fronting is, therefore, a specialised type of reinsurance, although historically
it has not always been viewed as such, especially when the risk is transferred
to another direct insurer. In the circumstances, to provide absolute clarity,
the Act specifies fronting arrangements as one of the issues that may be
provided for in directives (section 198(2)(l)).
111. Fronting carries several regulatory risks. These include the following:
(a) Although the economic risk is transferred from the fronting insurer to
the other insurer (the accepting insurer), at law the risk is carried by
the fronting insurer. The fronting insurer, which usually receives a
relatively small commission, is not paid enough to carry this risk.
65

(b) Fronting arrangements carry significant counterparty risk as the
fronting insurer is reliant on the accepting insurer with respect to the
payment of any claims. If the fronting arrangement does not take place
within the framework for reinsurance set out in the Act and the
directive, the Commission (and almost certainly the fronting insurer)
cannot be satisfied that the accepting insurer has the financial strength
to meet any claims made under the policy.
(c) If the fronting insurer is not paid, taking legal proceedings against the
accepting insurer in a foreign jurisdiction will usually be an extremely
expensive and uncertain process. In the meantime, the fronting insurer
remains fully liable to policyholders in Ghana for any claims.
(d) Fronting weakens the Commission’s control of the insurance market,
particularly where the accepting insurer is located outside Ghana. As
the accepting insurer carries the ultimate risk, policyholders in Ghana
are not fully protected.
(e) Fronting arrangements do not facilitate the development of expertise
within Ghana as the technical underwriting work is often done by the
foreign insurer outside the country.
112. For the above reasons, fronting is regarded as a form of reinsurance and
therefore subject to the requirements of the Act and the directive with respect
to reinsurance paragraph. Paragraph 58(2)(b) of the Act prohibits any
fronting arrangements where the accepting insurer is a direct insurer.
113. No account will be taken of any fronting arrangement that does not comply
with the directive for the purpose of calculating the capital requirements of
the fronting insurer.
114. Paragraph 56 of the directive defines a fronting arrangement as “an
arrangement through which an insurer cedes to another direct insurer or
reinsurer (whether or not licensed under the Act), the entire risk, or a
significant portion of the risk, under an insurance contract that it has entered
into, while remaining liable under the insurance contract to the insured.”.
This raises the question as to what is a “significant portion of the risk”.
115. It is difficult to set a specific retention level across the board as different
retention levels are appropriate for different classes and types of insurance.
However, the Commission considers that it would be difficult to justify ceding
more than 90% of the risk. However, this is not clear cut as 10% of a very
large risk may still be too high.
116. In considering whether a contract is fronting, the Commission also expects a
licensed insurer to adequately price the risk retained not to simply agree a
commission. Where the net retention is low, a licensed insurer should be
prepared to justify to the Commission proper pricing of the risk retained.
Insurance and Reinsurance Pools
117. Insurance pools are usually established to enable insurers to cover risks for
which they would not have individual capacity, to enable insurers, by pooling
risks, to gain access to lower reinsurance costs or for both reasons. The
establishment of a pool may also result in efficiencies that reduce the
66

technical and administrative expenses for individual insurers, but the
Commission considers that an arrangement for the sharing of technical and
administrative expenses alone is not a pooling arrangement. There must be a
sharing of insurance risk. Similarly, an arrangement that does not include
any sharing of premiums, expenses, losses and profits is more likely a simple
coinsurance arrangement rather than a pool.
118. Insurance pools can take a number of forms. Many insurance and reinsurance
pools are purely contractual in nature. However, as indicated in paragraph
57 of the directive, an insurance pool may be operated through a separate
legal entity established for the purpose and owned by the participating
(re)insurers. Where an insurance pool is established through a legal entity,
the legal entity will typically perform one of two functions. Either the risk will
be passed directly to the pool entity, which will write the insurance contracts
as insurer, or the participating insurers will each write the insurance
contracts but will be required to reinsure them to the pool vehicle.
119. Where the insurance pool operates through a legal entity established for the
purpose, and the pool entity either writes or reinsures the insurance
contracts, the entity acts as a risk carrier in its own right (either as a direct
insurer or as a reinsurer) and will need the appropriate licence under the Act.
In this case, exactly the same criteria would apply as with any other insurer
or reinsurer. The pool vehicle would have to be fully capitalised and comply
with all requirements of the Act.
120. Insurers participating in a contractual insurance pool may establish a
separate entity for purposes other than to act as a risk carrier. For example,
the legal entity may be established as the pool manager and/or to provide
technical, administrative and back-office functions for the participating
insurers. In that case, the entity may be established as an ordinary company,
or as any other type of entity permitted under the law. In these circumstances,
the entity would not require an insurers or reinsurers licence. However, if the
legal entity undertakes an activity that is otherwise licensable, such as
distributing the insurance contracts on behalf of the participating insurers, it
will of course require the appropriate intermediary licence.
Alternative Risk Transfer Arrangements
121. The term “alternative risk transfer arrangement” is defined as a form of risk
transfer by an insurer, other than through a traditional reinsurance
agreement. An alternative risk transfer arrangement seeks to achieve the
same economic effect as reinsurance, by transferring insurance risk away
from insurers, but by non-traditional methods. The arrangement must include
at least an element of insurance risk, rather than pure financial risk. In
summary, alternative risk transfer arrangements purport to transfer risk from
an insurer through an arrangement that does not possess the characteristics
required for a reinsurance contract. The risk is often, although not
necessarily, transferred to the capital markets. The risk may be transferred
to a reinsurer, but otherwise than through a reinsurance contract. The
definition in paragraph 58 sets out a non-exclusive list of different types of
alternative risk transfer mechanisms which are described briefly in the
67

following paragraphs. There are other forms alternative risk transfer
arrangement (ART), and ART continues to evolve.
122. Insurance-linked securities (or ILS): Insurance-linked securities or ILS is
an umbrella term that refers to a type of financial instrument the value of
which is affected by an insured loss event. There are various types of ILS,
including catastrophe bonds which are discussed further below. Insurance-
linked securities are typically sold through the capital markets to investors
who wish to diversify their risk. They are attractive to investors as the risks
under an insurance-linked security are not correlated with the financial
markets as their value is linked to non-financial risks, such as natural
disasters or longevity risk.
123. Catastrophe bonds: A catastrophe bond is issued by an insurer or reinsurer
to transfer its catastrophe risk under (re)insurance contracts that it
underwrites to the capital markets. Catastrophe bonds are typically issued
through a special purpose reinsurance company that issues a reinsurance
contract to one or more insurers to protect the (re)insurers against their
catastrophe risk. The special purpose reinsurer collateralises its obligations
under the reinsurance contract with the proceeds of a catastrophe bond. The
bondholders (usually institutional investors) receive interest on the
catastrophe bond during its term (usually 3 to 4 years). In the event of a
specified catastrophic event occurring within the term of the bond, the
investors will lose a part of the principal invested, or the entire principal
invested. Loss of principal may be triggered by the fact that the issuer has
incurred obligations under its (re)insurance contract or by a pre-determined
loss model or even a parametric index. If the catastrophe does not occur, the
principal is repaid to investors in full at the end of the term.
124. Reinsurance sidecars: Reinsurance sidecars are financial structure created
to allow investors to gain exposure to the risk and return of a group of
insurance policies or a book of business written by an insurer or reinsurer.
The capital invested is typically placed in trust (or in a special purpose
vehicle) and used to fully collateralise the contracts between the investors
and the ceding (re)insurers through which the investors share in the risk and
return on the underlying insurance policies or business (often through a
quota share arrangement).
The ceding (re)insurer will typically pay premiums for the coverage through
the sidecar up-front (to the trust or special purpose vehicle) allowing
investors to profit from the premium return but leaving their collateral
exposed for the duration of the underlying (re)insurance contracts. Typically,
the liability of investors is limited to the capital invested in the funds.
125. Industry loss warranties (or ILWs): Industry loss warranties (ILWs) are
financial instruments, which are issued in many forms, including reinsurance
contracts and derivatives, through which an insurer can obtain coverage on
the basis of industry losses rather than the losses arising from a specific event.
For example, an insurer writes property insurance in a market that is
infrequently hit by floods. Under this example, the insurer pays a premium
to the party providing the cover (which may be a reinsurer or, for example, a
hedge fund) and in return would receive payment if the industry losses
exceeded $5 billion through flood.
68

126. Finite reinsurance: Finite reinsurance is a type of reinsurance that transfers
a finite or limited amount of risk to the reinsurer. Risk is reduced through
accounting or financial methods, along with the actual transfer of economic
risk. By transferring less risk to the reinsurer, the insurer receives coverage
on its potential claims at a lower cost than traditional reinsurance.
127. As these arrangements are intended to provide an alternative to traditional
reinsurance, with the possibility that the counterparty is not a traditional
foreign or licensed reinsurer, they expose a licensed insurer using them to
some additional risks. For this reason, alternative risk transfer arrangements
are subject to approval by the Commission on a case-by-case basis.
128. Alternative risk transfer arrangements can be sophisticated and complex. A
licensed insurer that applies for consent to use an alternative risk transfer
mechanism will be expected to satisfy the Commission that it has a sufficient
understanding of the mechanism and the risks to which it is exposed and to
demonstrate its effectiveness in transferring risk from the insurer.
129. The Commission may approve alternative risk transfer arrangements on a
case-by-case basis. In considering an application for approval, the
Commission will need to be satisfied that the arrangements achieve risk
transfer, that the arrangements are transparent and the cedant understands
and has mitigated the attendant credit, liquidity and reputational risks
associated with the arrangement. The Commission is very unlikely to approve
any arrangement where the other party to the arrangement is not supervised
to the Commission’s satisfaction.
Part 4 – Conduct of Business
Preliminary
Application of this Part
60. This Part does not apply to a licensed reinsurer and a reference in this Part
to a licensed insurer shall not be taken to include a reference to a licensed reinsurer.
Meaning of “bundled insurance product”
61. (1) A bundled insurance product is an insurance product that comprises
two or more insurance contracts that are sold together as a single insurance product.
(2) Without limiting subparagraph (1), a bundled insurance product may
comprise
(a) two or more insurance contracts, each of which constitutes general
business; or
(b) two or more insurance contracts, each of which constitutes long term
business; or
(c) one or more insurance contracts that constitute general business and
one or more insurance contracts that constitute long term business.
(3) If an insurance contract that constitutes general business is bundled
with an insurance contract that constitutes long term business
69

(a) the insurance contract that constitutes general business must be
underwritten by a licensed insurer that is authorised to carry on
general business of the relevant class; and
(b) the insurance contract that constitutes long term business must be
underwritten by a licensed insurer that is authorised to carry on long
term business of the relevant class.
(4) Unless provided otherwise, a bundled insurance product must be
treated as a single insurance contract, provided that any obligations imposed
on a licensed insurer must be treated as imposed on each insurer that
underwrites an insurance contract that is part of the bundled insurance product.
Meaning of “distribute” in relation to an insurance contract
62. A licensed insurer distributes an insurance contract if the licensed insurer
(a) solicits applications for, negotiates or concludes the insurance
contract
(i) solely through its own sales representatives; or
(ii) through an insurance intermediary; or
(b) enters into a group insurance contract with a master policyholder.
Retail customers
63. If a licensed insurer is not certain whether a customer or prospective
customer is a retail customer or a commercial customer, it must treat the customer
or prospective customer as a retail customer.
GUIDELINES
Objectives
130. The requirements and obligations in this Part are intended
(a) to protect the customers and prospective customers of insurers and to
promote fair outcomes for customers;
(b) to strengthen public trust and consumer confidence in the insurance
sector;
(c) to minimise the risk that insurers will follow business models that are
unsustainable or pose reputational risk to individual insurers and to the
insurance industry as a whole; and
(d) to support a sound and resilient insurance sector by creating a level
playing field on which insurers can compete, while maintaining
business practices that support the fair treatment of customers.
Definitions
131. There are a number of important definitions relevant to the conduct of
business in the Act and the Regulations. For ease of use, these are set out
below.
132. In the case of a licensed insurer:
70

(a) the Act defines “customer” as a policyholder of the insurer or a
beneficiary under an insurance contract entered into by the insurer;
and
(b) the Regulations define “beneficiary” as a person, other than the
policyholder, who is entitled to receive a payment or other benefit under
an insurance contract or who, on the occurrence of the insured event,
is entitled to make a claim against the insurer under the insurance
contract.
133. The Regulations define
(a) a “retail customer” as a customer of an insurer who enters into a retail
insurance contract with the insurer;
(b) a “retail insurance contract” as an insurance contract entered into by
an individual wholly or mainly for purposes unrelated to the
individual’s trade, business or profession; and
(c) a “commercial customer” as any customer of an insurer who is not a
retail customer.
134. Retail customers may be expected to have a more limited knowledge and
understanding of insurance and about the legal rights and obligations arising
from an insurance contract than commercial customers. There is also likely
to be a greater asymmetry of information between a licensed insurer and a
retail customer than between a licensed insurer and a commercial customer.
Retail customers therefore have different needs in terms of consumer
protection than commercial customers. The directive reflects this by imposing
stronger consumer protection requirements on licensed insurers with respect
to their retail customers.
135. Private individuals may act in a number of different capacities. Although the
capacity in which an individual acts will usually be clear, this will not always
be the case. For example, an individual seeking motor insurance may use the
vehicle to be insured for both business and non-business purposes. If the
predominant use of the vehicle is personal, or the insurer is in any doubt as
to whether the use is predominantly personal or business, the individual must
be treated as a retail customer. Given the potential lack of clarity, paragraph
63 of the directive provides that should there be any doubt, the customer must
be treated as a retail customer.
136. Similarly, it is possible for the same individual to be treated as a retail
customer in respect of one insurance contract and as a commercial customer
in respect of another insurance contract. For example, an individual may
insure his or her office premises separately from his or her home. In relation
to the insurance contract that covers the office premises, the individual will
be treated as a commercial customer but in relation to the domestic insurance
policy, the individual will be treated as a retail customer.
Bundled insurance product
137. The term “bundled insurance product” is used to describe an insurance
contract that includes two or more separate insurance contracts. It is not
71

intended to cover insurance contracts that are sold together, or bundled, with
other types of financial products.
General Obligations
General obligations
64. (1) A licensed insurer must
(a) have due regard for the interests and needs of its customers;
(b) treat its customers and prospective customers fairly;
(c) identify and avoid or properly manage conflict of interest fairly,
whether the conflicts arise between itself and its customers or
prospective customers or between different customers or
prospective customers;
(d) pay due regard to the information needs of its customers and
prospective customers;
(e) take reasonable steps to ensure that information is communicated to
its customers and prospective customers in a way that is clear and
fair and that is not inaccurate or misleading; and
(f) ensure that customer information is adequately protected and used
appropriately.
(2) In relation to a particular customer or prospective customer, the
obligations under
(a) subparagraph (1)(a) to (e) of this Directive and section 84(1)(a) and
(b) of the Act apply from before a contract of insurance is entered
into until, where a prospective customer becomes a customer, all
obligations under the contract have been satisfied;
(b) subparagraph (1)(f) of this Directive applies in respect of customer
information relating to former customers or former prospective
customers until the licensed insurer no longer holds or controls the
information.
Business conduct policies, procedures and controls
65. (1) The board of a licensed insurer must ensure that the insurer has documented
business conduct policies, procedures and controls in place with the objective of
achieving compliance with the conduct of business requirements of the Act, the
Regulations and the directives.
(2) The business conduct policies, procedures and controls must take
account of
(a) the circumstances of different customers and prospective customers,
including whether customers and prospective customers are, or
would be, retail customers or commercial customers; and
(b) the experience and expertise of different customers and prospective
customers, the information available to them and the needs that
different customers and prospective customers have for advice.
72

(3) Without limiting this paragraph, the business conduct policies and
procedures of a licensed insurer must cover or include the following
(a) measures to enable it to meet its general conduct of business
obligations specified in section 84 of the Act and paragraph 64 of
the Directive;
(b) the development, marketing and sale of insurance products, with the
objective that due regard is given to the interests and needs of
different types of customers and prospective customers;
(c) the provision of clear information to customers and prospective
customers at the point of sale and before and after an insurance
contract is entered into;
(d) measures aimed at minimising the risk that insurance products sold
to customers are inappropriate for their needs;
(e) where advice is given to customers and prospective customers,
measures aimed at ensuring that the advice is of high quality;
(f) procedures for dealing with customer claims, complaints and
disputes in a fair and timely manner;
(g) the protection and appropriate use of customer information; and
(h) the management of the reasonable expectations of customers.
(4) A licensed insurer must take appropriate measures to ensure that
(a) the fair treatment of customers and prospective customers is an
integral part of its business culture; and
(b) its employees and agents meet high standards of ethics and integrity.
GUIDELINES
General Conduct of Business Obligations
138. Section 84 of the Act sets out a number of general conduct of business
obligations that apply to all licensed insurers. These are supplemented by the
obligations set out in paragraph 64 of the Directive. It is not possible to cover
every situation in the Act, Regulations and Directive and where specific
circumstances are not covered, the Commission requires licensed insurers to
have regard to and comply with the general obligations in the Act and the
Directive. If a particular situation requires higher standards than the Act or
directives require to meet the overriding obligations, licensed insurers must
apply the higher standards.
Conflicts of interest
139. Paragraph 64(1)(c) requires an insurer to identify and avoid or manage
conflict of interest fairly, between itself and its customers or between its
customers. A conflict of interest with respect to a customer creates a risk that
an insurer will not give proper consideration to the customer’s interests and
that this may lead the insurer to treat the customer unfairly.
73

140. In the context of conduct of business, conflict of interest may arise from
inappropriate remuneration or compensation structures, other financial and
non-financial incentives and performance targets or performance
management criteria. These may result, for example, in the sale of products
that are not appropriate for a customer’s needs. It is important to appreciate
that the duties of an insurer extend to the conflict that may arise between
those acting for it and its customers. In designing its commission structures,
offering inducements to its sales staff, insurance agents and insurance
brokers and setting performance targets or performance management
criteria, a licensed insurer should consider whether these create conflict of
interest between those whom it seeks to reward and its customers (and
prospective customers) that would cause it to breach its obligations to act
with integrity and to treat its customers fairly. Inducements include any
benefit offered to sales staff, insurance agents or insurance brokers that
incentivise the person to adopt a particular course of action, and may include
commission, cash, cash equivalents, goods, hospitality or training
programmes.
141. It may be possible to manage a conflict of interest through appropriate
disclosure, enabling a customer or prospective customer to determine
whether a sale may be influenced by financial or non-financial incentives.
However, disclosure cannot be relied upon as a method of managing conflict
of interest unless the customer or prospective customer is able to understand
