the significance of the conflict. Given the imbalance of knowledge and
understanding between insurers (and insurance intermediaries) and their
customers, particularly retail customers, disclosure is subject to significant
limitations as a method of managing conflict of interest.
142. If a conflict of interests cannot be managed satisfactorily, a licensed insurer
should decline to act.
Customer information
143. “Customer information” is defined as including information “provided by or
relating to” customers and prospective customers. Customer information
therefore extends well beyond information provided by a customer or
prospective customer. It includes all information collected, held, used and
communicated by and to third parties that relates to a customer or
prospective customer.
144. Much of this information is sensitive and confidential (for example, financial,
medical and health information). The Commission expects licensed insurers
to have strong procedures in place to ensure the protection and appropriate
use of customer information. The Commission expects the policies and
procedures to extend through all levels of the insurer and that the risks
associated with the misuse of information will be included within the risk
management framework.
Business Conduct Policies, Procedures and Controls
145. Strong business conduct requirements and standards are important not just
to protect customers and prospective customers at an individual level, but
also to strengthen trust and consumer confidence in the insurance sector,
74

which is a pre-requisite for the future growth and development of the Ghana
insurance market.
146. The Commission expects that all staff of the licensed insurer will be trained
on the policies and procedures as will any intermediary that is dealing with
a customer or prospective customer on behalf of the insurer.
Fair Treatment of Customers
147. To ensure compliance with the directive, it is important that the fair treatment
of customers is embedded within the corporate culture and values of an
insurer. This requires the fair treatment of customers to be considered in the
design of the insurer’s business strategy, to be a central part of the
development, design, marketing and sale of insurance products and to be
taken into account in the development of the insurer’s procedures and
controls. The board and senior management have overall responsibility for
the fair treatment of customers, including setting the tone for the insurer.
Ethics and Integrity
148. Paragraph 65(4)(b) requires a licensed insurer to take appropriate measures
to ensure that its employees and agents meet high standards of ethics and
integrity. This requires not just that staff are appropriately trained, but also
that the insurer places emphasis on this when recruiting staff and that the
remuneration structures support this.
149. The Commission considers that appropriate measures under paragraph
65(4)(b) should include the development of a code of ethics, or equivalent
document, that sets out what the insurer considers to be acceptable and
unacceptable behaviour with the intention of embedding the fair treatment of
customers into the corporate culture.
Insurance Products
Development of insurance products
66. (1) A licensed insurer must, when designing and developing insurance
products
(a) take account of any product development criteria or Guidance issued
by the Commission; and
(b) have regard to the interests of different types of customers and
prospective customers.
(2) A licensed insurer must
(a) ensure that every new product is subject to an internal review
process that includes
(i) a review against the relevant requirements of the Act, this
directive and any product development criteria or Guidance
issued by the Commission;
(ii) a review against the insurer’s business strategy and objectives
and its risk management strategy and policies; and
75

(iii) an actuarial review undertaken by the head of the actuarial
function or the appointed actuary covering the commission rates
and the adequacy of the premium rates.
(b) make and retain written records that demonstrate its compliance
with subparagraph (a).
(3) Every new insurance product must be approved by senior
management or the board of the licensed insurer
Requirements relating to group insurance contracts
67. (1) A group insurance policy document must state the insurable interest of
the master policyholder.
(2) The terms of a group insurance contract must require the master
policyholder to
(a) maintain a register of beneficiaries under the contract which must
(i) adequately identify each beneficiary;
(ii) record the date upon which the person became a beneficiary and
the date on which the beneficiary was provided with a copy of
the Policy Summary;
(iii) provide details of any other persons, including members of the
beneficiary’s family, who are entitled to benefits under the
contract by virtue of the person becoming a beneficiary; and
(iv) if beneficiaries are able to exercise options to take different
levels of cover, summarise the cover provided to the beneficiary
by the contract;
(b) provide each person who becomes a beneficiary under a group
insurance contract with
(i) a copy of the Policy Summary;
(ii) if not specified on the Policy Summary, a Schedule setting out
the details of the cover provided to the beneficiary;
(iii) the name and contact details of an employee or representative of
the policyholder whom the beneficiary may contact for further
information in relation to the contract; and
(iv) details as to how the beneficiary may access a copy of the policy
document.
(3) A licensed insurer must take reasonable steps to ensure that the
master policyholder complies with the obligations specified in subparagraph
(2).
Bundled insurance products
68. (1) In the case of a bundled insurance product of the type specified in paragraph
61(2)(c), the licensed insurers proposing to offer the bundled product must enter
into a written agreement providing for the terms of the arrangement, which must
include
(a) the designation of one of the licensed insurers as the lead licensed
insurer and the responsibilities of the lead licensed insurer;
76

(b) the basis on which premiums and responsibility for claims will be
allocated between the licensed insurers; and
(c) any commission, charges or other consideration to be paid to the lead
licensed insurer.
(2) The responsibilities of the lead licensed insurer must include
(a) the receipt of all premiums payable under the product and the
payment of the agreed allocation of the premium to the other
licensed insurer or licensed insurers;
(b) the receipt, management and, in consultation with the other licensed
insurer or licensed insurers, the settlement and payment of all claims
made under the product.
Cancellation by retail customers
69. (1) A retail insurance contract must provide the policyholder with a right to
cancel the contract without giving any reason and without any fee or penalty within
14 days or the latter of
(a) the date that the contract is entered into; or
(b) the date on which the policyholder receives the policy
documentation.
(2) Subparagraph (1) does not apply
(a) to a general insurance contract, where the insured period is one
month or less;
(b) if the policyholder or a beneficiary has made a claim under the
contract;
(c) to an insurance contract, the performance of which has been fully
completed by both parties at the request of the policyholder or a
beneficiary, before the policyholder exercises the right to cancel the
contract; or
(d) to an index insurance contract.
(3) A retail insurance contract must specify the procedures for effecting
cancellation within the 14-day period specified in subparagraph (1) and
provide that, on the policyholder complying with those procedures
(a) the contract is terminated; and
(b) the amount required to be paid by the policyholder must be no more
than the cost of the insurance cover provided, on a proportionate
basis, for the period of cover and no penalty or fee must be payable
by the customer.
(4) When a retail customer exercises his or her right to cancel under
terms required by this paragraph, the licensed insurer concerned must repay
the balance of the premium paid by the retail customer promptly.
Cancellation permitted by insurance contract
70. (1) If a contract of insurance, whether retail or commercial, provides the
policyholder, the licensed insurer or both with rights to cancel the insurance
contract, additional to those specified in paragraph 69, the contract must specify
77

(a) the cancellation rights;
(b) the procedures for the cancellation of the insurance contract; and
(c) the consequences of cancellation.
(2) If, under a retail insurance contract, a licensed insurer provides
longer or additional cancellation rights to those required under paragraph 69,
the longer or additional cancellation rights must be on terms that are at least
as favourable to retail customers as those provided by paragraph 69.
(3) An insurance contract must clearly state the consequences for
cancellation of an insurance contract
(a) by a retail customer, after the end of the period specified in
paragraph 69(1) or beyond the terms of any additional or extended
cancellation rights provided by the contract; and
(b) by a commercial customer, beyond the terms of any cancellation
rights provided by the contract.
Reinstatement of life insurance contract
71. (1) For the purposes of this paragraph
“covered risk” means a risk that occurs during the reinstatement period
of a covered life contract that has not been renewed or that has lapsed due
to the non-payment of the premium, that would have given rise to a claim
had the covered life contract
(a) been renewed; or
(b) not lapsed;
“covered life contract” means a life insurance contract that is renewable
annually or in respect of which premiums are payable annually;
“reinstatment period” means a period of 14 days commencing on
(a) the renewal date of a covered life contract which is renewable
annually; or
(b) the latest date for payment of a premium that, under a covered
life contract, is payable annually.
(2) A covered life contract must
(a) provide for the automatic reinstatement of the covered life contract
from the first day of the reinstatement period, if the renewal or
annual premium due is paid on or before the last day of the
reinstatement period;
(b) if the covered life contract is reinstated, permit a claim to be made
for any covered risk that occurs during the reinstatement period.
(3) A covered life contract must be reinstated under this paragraph
(a) on the same terms as would have applied had the renewal or annual
premium been paid on or before the due date; and
(b) even if a covered event occurs during the reinstatement period.
78

Approval of insurance products
72. (1) A licensed insurer must not market or sell an insurance product unless
the Commission has approved the product.
(2) This paragraph does not apply to an insurance product that
(a) has been approved by, or is covered by an approval of, the
Commission prior to the Act coming into force;
(b) is substantively equivalent to an insurance product referred to in
paragraph (a); or
(c) the directive permits a licensed insurer to market and sell on a “no
objection” or “file and use” basis.
(3) A licensed insurer may apply to the Commission for the approval of
(a) an insurance contract, including a group insurance contract; or
(b) two or more insurance contracts as a bundled insurance product.
(4) In the case of a bundled insurance product of the type specified in
paragraph 61(2)(c), the application for approval must be made by the lead
licensed insurer.
(5) An application under subparagraph (1) must be in, and contain the
information specified in, the form approved by the Commission and must be
accompanied by
(a) copies of the proposed insurance contract or of each insurance
contract in a bundled insurance product, the policy document, any
riders or endorsements and the proposal form;
(b) details of the premium and commission rates;
(c) an actuarial memorandum on the proposed insurance contract or
bundled insurance product signed by the head of the actuarial
function or the appointed actuary;
(d) a statement of approval signed by the chief executive officer, on
behalf of senior management, or a director on behalf of the board.
(e) copies of the proposed marketing material, including the proposed
Policy Summary produced in accordance with paragraph 77;
(f) details of how it is proposed that the insurance product will be
distributed;
(g) the proposed reinsurance arrangements or if no reinsurance
arrangements are proposed, a statement to that effect;
(h) in the case of a bundled insurance product of a type referred to in
paragraph 61(2)(c), a copy of the agreement entered into, or
proposed to be entered into, between the licensed insurers

(i) in the case of a branded product or a co-branded product, a copy of

(6) The Commission may require a licensed insurer to provide it with
such information and documents, in addition to those specified in subparagraph
(3), as it reasonably requires to determine the application.
(7) If, before the determination by the Commission of an application for

(a) there is a material change in any information or documentation

(b) the licensed insurer discovers that any such information or

the licensed insurer must immediately give the Commission written particulars of

Limitations of approval

a licensed insurer and its board have responsibility for all insurance products
designed, developed, marketed and sold by the insurer and for ensuring that its
products are appropriate and comply with the requirements of the Act, the
Regulations and the Directive.
(2) The approval by the Commission of an insurance product is not to be
taken as an assurance that
(a) the technical aspects of the product, including the pricing, have been

(b) the development and design of the product is appropriate for those
to whom it is intended to be marketed; or
(c) that the product complies with the requirements of the Act, this

Revocation of approval

(a) on the application of the licensed insurer; or
(b) if the Commission considers that the insurance contract or bundled
insurance product
(i) does not comply with the requirements of the Act, the
Regulations or the Directive or no longer satisfies, or never
satisfied, its product development criteria and any Guidelines on

(ii) is not being marketed or sold in accordance with the Act, the

(iii) it is in the interests of customers or prospective customers of the

GUIDELINES
Product Development
150. In some insurance markets, it is not unusual for intermediaries (including
insurance brokers, technical service providers, consulting actuaries and
reinsurers) to be heavily involved in the development of insurance products
for insurers. The involvement of intermediaries, particularly technical service
providers, is becoming more prevalent in Ghana, especially in respect of
microinsurance products and insurance products distributed over mobile
networks. Where a licensed insurer underwrites a product developed by an
intermediary or other third party, the Commission expects the insurer to
retain oversight of the product’s development and will hold the insurer
accountable for its development.
151. Paragraph 66(2)(a) requires a licensed insurer to ensure that each new
product goes through an internal review process. The Commissions expects
the review process to cover matters such as whether
(a) the product
(i) delivers the reasonably expected benefits; and
(ii) targets the customers for whose needs the product is likely to be
appropriate, while preventing, or limiting, access by customers
for whom the product is likely to be inappropriate;
(b) the distribution methods are appropriate for the product; and
(c) advice should be provided.
Cancellation Rights
152. Paragraph 69 requires a licensed insurer to give a retail customer the right
to cancel an insurance contract during a 14-day cooling off period. A retail
customer who cancels the contract must be given a full refund of the premium
paid, less a charge equal to the cost of the insurance cover provided for the
period of cover. The paragraph provides for this to be calculated on a
proportionate basis. The Commission expects that, during the cooling off
period, the calculation of the premium payable will be at the same premium
rate as that applying to the contract. The Commission would not regard as
fair a charge based, for example, on a short-term contract rate. Although it
may be appropriate for a licensed insurer to charge an administration fee for
the exercise of a cancellation right outside the cooling off period, the
Commission does not consider this appropriate during the cooling off period.
Paragraph 69(1) provides for this.
153. Paragraph 70(2) provides that, if a licensed insurer provides a retail
customer with additional or extended cancellation rights to those required
during the cooling off period, the longer or additional cancellation rights
must be on terms that are at least as favourable to retail customers as those
81

provided by paragraph 69. This is not intended to require a licensed insurer
to provide equivalent terms throughout an extended cancellation period, but
it cannot through extended or additional cancellation rights reduce the
cancellation rights of the retail customer during the cooling off period.
154. In considering whether to approve an insurance product, the Commission will
review the terms relating to cancellation to satisfy itself that they are
reasonable and fair and that there is adequate disclosure concerning any fees
payable. In the case of a life insurance contract, the Commission expects the
insurer to disclose fully the consequences of early cancellation by the
policyholder, including (to the extent applicable):
(a) the risk that the policyholder will lose the initial premium; and
(b) the likelihood that the policyholder will not receive a refund or other
payment.
Approval of Insurance Contracts
155. Terms that seek to exclude the liability of an insurer can be disadvantageous
and unfair to customers. Exclusion clauses can also impact negatively on the
reputation of an insurer, and on insurance as a product. The Commission
therefore expects insurers to seek to exclude liability only where it is
reasonable to do so. This is a factor that the Commission will consider in
determining whether to approve a product.
156. For the purposes of Paragraph 72(2), the Commission considers any
additions or modification to the product’s exclusions or endorsements or any
changes affecting the rights of customers would be sufficient to require an
application for approval, as the product would no longer be considered
“substantively equivalent”.
157. In the case of an application for the approval of a bundled insurance product
of the type specified in paragraph 61(2)(c), the Commission expects that in
most cases, the actuarial report would be prepared and signed by the head of
the actuarial function or the appointed actuary of the lead licensed insurer.
However, this may not be appropriate if the work on which the report was
based was undertaken by the actuarial function or appointed actuary of
another of the licensed insurers that will underwrite the product. The
Commission expects a statement of approval under section 72(5)(d) to be
provided by, or signed on behalf of, each of the licensed insurers.
158. When assessing an application by a licensed insurer for approval of an
insurance product, the Commission will expect the insurer to demonstrate
that it has taken reasonable steps to ensure that
(a) the product will deliver the reasonably expected benefits;
(b) the product will be targeted only at those customers for whose needs
the product is likely to be appropriate; and
(c) the proposed distribution channels are appropriate for the insurance
product.
82

Revocation of approval
159. Before revoking an approval under paragraph 74(b), the Commission will
usually give the licensed insurer a written notice of intended revocation
stating the grounds for revoking the approval. The Commission will give the
licensed insurer a period of at least 14 days to provide a response.
160. The Commission will revoke the approval if
(a) it does not receive a response within the 14 days period; or
(b) having received a response, it decides that the approval should be
revoked anyway.
161. The Commission may decide that it is in the interests of customers or
prospective customers that the approval should be revoked with immediate
effect, in which case the approval will be revoked without giving the licensed
insurer notice of intended revocation.
Distribution of Insurance Products
Marketing of insurance products
75. A licensed insurer must
(a) take into account the interests of different types of customers and
prospective customers when marketing an insurance product;
(b) take reasonable steps to ensure that its products are promoted to
customers and prospective customers in a way that
(i) is clear and fair and that is not inaccurate or misleading; and
(ii) takes account of the knowledge and experience of a typical
customer for the insurance product being marketed;
(c) take reasonable steps to ensure that
(i) a customer or prospective customer knows whether or not
advice is being provided;
(ii) any advice that the licensed insurer provides to a customer or
prospective customer is appropriate, taking into account the
circumstances disclosed to it by that person; and
(iii) a person only purchases an insurance product if the person is
eligible to obtain benefits under the product;
(d) provide relevant information to its sales staff and any insurance
intermediaries through which it distributes the products, so as to
ensure that they understand the target market and the characteristics
of the product; and
(e) monitor the performance of the product, and its distribution, after
marketing has commenced, including in relation to
(i) its suitability for the consumers for whom it was developed and
to whom it is marketed;
83

(ii) whether the product is continuing to deliver the expected
benefits; and
(iii) whether the proposed distribution channels are appropriate for
the product; and
(f) monitor compliance with paragraphs (b), (c) and (d).
Promotional material
76. (1) Any promotional material that a licensed insurer prepares in relation to
an insurance product must
(a) identify the insurer as the underwriter of the product;
(b) identify any coinsurers that underwrite the product;
(c) state prominently the basis for any claimed benefits and any
significant limitations;
(d) be consistent with the coverage provided by the product; and
(e) not hide, diminish or obscure important statements or warnings.
(2) A licensed insurer must take reasonable care to ensure that any
promotional material referred to in subparagraph (1) is easily understandable
by those persons to whom the product or the promotional material is targeted.
(3) A licensed insurer must, in the insurance contract and in all
promotional and other material that it issues state that the insurer is regulated
by the Commission under the Insurance Act.
Policy summary
77. (1) A licensed insurer must prepare a Policy Summary complying with this
paragraph in relation to every retail insurance contract that it markets and sells,
including a branded or co-branded insurance contract, and may prepare a Policy
Summary in relation to any commercial insurance contract that it markets and sells.
(2) A Policy Summary must
(a) be written in plain language and take into account the likely level of
understanding of insurance of the target market for the contract;
(b) contain a summary of the cover provided by, and the key features
of, the insurance contract; and
(c) clearly state that it is a Policy Summary prepared in accordance with
this directive.
(3) Without limiting subparagraph (2), the Policy Summary must contain
the following information
(a) the name of the insurer and the address of its principal office in
Ghana;
(b) the type of insurance contract;
(c) a description of the risks insured by the contract and any significant
or unusual exclusions or limitations;
(d) the duration of the policy, stating whether it is a general or long term
insurance contract;
84

(e) the policy benefits, including any policy limits and any excess that
may be payable by the policyholder;
(f) details of the policyholder’s cancellation rights and a brief summary
of those rights including their duration;
(g) the grace period for payment of premiums, if any;
(h) the consequences for surrender or early termination by the
policyholder otherwise than in accordance with the cancellation
rights;
(i) the contact details for notifying a claim under the policy and a brief
summary of the claims procedure;
(j) the obligations on a prospective customer to disclose material facts;
(k) where appropriate, a statement that the policyholder may need to
review and update the cover periodically to ensure that it remains
adequate;
(l) the right to complain and the method of lodging a complaint; and
(m) a statement that the Policy Summary does not contain the full terms
of the insurance contract, which are to be found in the policy
document.
(4) For the purposes of subparagraph (3)(c)
(a) a significant exclusion or limitation is one that would tend to affect
the decision of a prospective policyholder who would be a retail
customer, or retail customers generally, to purchase the insurance
contract; and
(b) an unusual exclusion or limitation is one that would not usually be
included in a comparable insurance contract.
(5) The Policy Summary must not contain any information other than the

Branded insurance products
78. If an insurance contract is distributed as a branded product, the Policy

(a) state that the contract is underwritten by a licensed insurer; and
(b) specify the licensed insurer concerned.
Provision of Policy Summary or information by licensed insurer
79. (1) If a licensed insurer deals or communicates directly with a person
concerning the sale or renewal of an insurance contract, the insurer must provide
the person with
(a) in the case of a retail insurance contract, the Policy Summary and
the additional information specified in subparagraph (2); or
(b) in the case of a commercial insurance contract
(i) a Policy Summary and the additional information specified in
subparagraph (2); or
85

(ii) appropriate information concerning the contract.
(2) Where a licensed insurer provides a person with a Policy Summary,
unless included in the Policy Summary, it must also provide that person with
the following additional information
(a) details of the premium payable, the date when the premium is
required to be paid and the consequences for non–payment of the
premium; and
(b) if an insurance contract is purchased in connection with other goods
or services, details of that part of the total price payable that

subparagraph (1) must be provided in sufficient time for the person to make an

and sign a statement, supported by the customer’s signature, that the customer

(6) An acknowledgement in writing must be signed by the customer or
if for any reason the customer is unable or unwilling to sign the

thumbprint.
Additional requirements, insurance contracts with investment component
80. (1) If a retail life insurance product includes an investment component, the
licensed insurer must, either in the Policy Summary or in a separate document
provided with the Policy Summary
(a) provide a brief description of the objectives of the product;
(b) state in general terms, whom the product is suitable for;
(c) specify the customer’s commitments;
(d) set out the material risks of the product;
(e) provide a summary of the main features of the product; and

(3) Projections and performance data should be prefaced with clear

(a) past experience is no guarantee of the level of future returns;
86

(b) any projections are illustrative examples and the actual return may

(c) the projections must be notional and not based on past performance.

Inaccurate, unclear, unfair or misleading material

issued, or a Policy Summary, is not clear or fair or is inaccurate or misleading, it

(b) in the case of the Policy Summary, amend it and, in the case of any

Electronic communications

(2) For the purposes of subparagraph (1), consent may be given by an

program.
(3) Consent under subparagraph (1) may also be given through assistive
technology systems or devices that are designed to enable persons with a visual
or other impairment or persons who are illiterate to understand the content of

(a) systems that enable consent to be securely given by another person
on behalf of a person with a visual or other impairment or of an

87

(b) software or systems that enable the communication of documents,
and the provision of consent, through text to speech software and

GUIDELINES
The Marketing of Insurance Products
162. Paragraph 75(b)(i) requires a licensed insurer to take reasonable steps to
ensure that its products are promoted to customers and prospective
customers in a way that is clear and fair and that is not inaccurate or
misleading. The Commission expects that, if promotional material is
prepared by an insurance intermediary or a third-party service provider on
the insurer’s behalf, the insurer will verify the accuracy of the promotional
material, as well as satisfying itself that the material will enable compliance
with paragraph 75(b)(i).
163. Paragraph 75(c)(i) and (ii) relate to the provision of advice to customers or
prospective customers. There is a clear distinction between the provision of
“advice” and the provision of information and explanations. Giving advice
involves making a recommendation based on the needs and circumstances of
the customer or prospective customer. A licensed insurer is not required to
provide advice, and it is therefore important that a customer or prospective
customer knows whether he or she is being provided with advice as opposed
to information and/or an explanation. For this reason, paragraph 75(c)(i)
therefore requires a licensed insurer to ensure that a customer or prospective
customer knows whether he or she is being provided with advice. If a licensed
insurer gives advice, paragraph 75(c)(ii) requires the insurer to “take
reasonable care” to ensure that any advice that it provides to a person is
appropriate, taking into account the circumstances disclosed to it by that
person. In assessing compliance with this obligation, the Commission would
expect to see evidence that the insurer has made enquiries of the policyholder
or prospective policyholder concerning his or her needs in relation to
insurance and relevant circumstances and that the disclosed needs and
circumstances have been considered.
164. Where advice is provided by a licensed insurer, the Commission expects the
insurer to document the advice provided and the basis on which it was given,
including the reasons for any recommendations made. The Commission also
expects licensed insurers to keep copies of any documents provided to a
customer or prospective customer.
165. Whether or not advice is provided, a licensed insurer is required to take
reasonable steps to ensure that a person only buys an insurance product if
the person is eligible to obtain benefits under the product. The Commission
takes a proportionate approach in determining whether a licensed insurer
has taken “reasonable steps”.
166. In the case of a standard insurance product, if the eligibility requirements are
typical or to be reasonably expected for the type of product, reasonable steps
88

may consist of no more than clearly highlighting any eligibility criteria and
requiring the prospective customer to acknowledge in writing that he or she
meets them. Examples could include:
(a) a travel insurance policy under which medical benefits are only payable
if the insured traveller is aged under 65 years; and
(b) a motor policy that only pays out if the insured driver holds a valid
driving licence.
167. In the case of insurance products that are complex or non-standard or include
unusual or exceptional eligibility criteria, the Commission would expect the
licensed insurer to undertake more extensive enquiries. For example, an
income protection policy that pays the insured an income for periods of illness
to cover loss of employment income which provides cover to employees but
not to persons who are self-employed.
168. If, before the sale is concluded, a licensed insurer discovers that the
prospective customer is eligible for some, but not all, of the benefits, it should
advise the prospective customer so that he or she can take an informed
decision on whether to buy the product. For example, under a property
insurance contract, the insurer discovers that the property is in a flood plain.
The prospective customer would not, therefore, be covered for flood damage
but would be covered for other types of property damage.
Policy Summary
169. Paragraph 77 requires a licensed insurer to prepare a Policy Summary for
every retail insurance contract that it markets or sells. A Policy Summary
serves two principal purposes. First, by setting out the main features of an
insurance product in clear and summary form, it should assist policyholders
and prospective policyholders to gain an understanding of the product.
Second, it assists policyholders and prospective policyholders to compare
insurance products offered by different licensed insurers. This assists in the
promotion of a competitive market.
170. The Commission expects a Policy Summary to:
(a) present information in a logical order, with appropriate use of headings
and sub-headings;
(b) as far as possible, avoid the use of jargons, unfamiliar or technical
language;
(c) if it is necessary to use jargons, unfamiliar or technical language,
provide accompanying explanations in plain language;
(d) use short sentences; and
(e) avoid duplication and unnecessary disclaimers.
A Policy Summary should not simply replicate the policy document but should
aim to provide a clear summary of the key features of the policy including all
the information set out in paragraph 77(3).
171. In order to assist customers to compare insurance products, it is important
that every Product Summary is prepared in standardised form and contains
the same categories of information. For this reason, paragraph 77(5)
89

requires that a Policy Summary shall not contain any information other than
the information provided for in that paragraph.
172. Paragraph 77(3)(c) requires a Policy Summary to set out any significant or
unusual exclusions or limitations. Examples of these could include:
(a) the exclusion of specific medical conditions, diseases or existing
medical conditions;
(b) any waiting period;
(c) limits on the period for which benefits will be paid;
(d) restrictions on eligibility to claim, such as age, employment status or
residence;
(e) ceilings and limits; and
(f) circumstances under which cover is not provided, such as loss or
damage to property caused by or resulting from acts or omissions of
the policyholder and risks not covered by the policy.
173. Paragraph 77(3)(c) requires a Policy Summary to state the contact details
for notifying a claim under the policy and to set out a brief summary of the
claims procedure. This should include instructions as to the actions to be
taken by a claimant in the event of an insured loss occurring.
174. Where a licensed insurer markets products electronically, the insurer must
place a copy of the relevant Policy Summaries on its website and draw the
attention of customers or prospective policyholders prior to concluding any
insurance contract.
Insurance products with an investment component
175. Paragraph 80 applies to life insurance products that provide benefits arising
from an investment. These may include, for example:
(a) investment-linked insurance policies, where the benefits payable under
the policy are wholly or partly determined by reference to the value of,
or the income from, property of any description or by reference to
fluctuations in, or in an index of, the value of property of any
description (also known as “unit linked policies”); and
(b) participating policies, which confer a right to participate in the profits
of the insurer or a specified asset fund, through bonuses allocated,
usually on an annual basis and sometimes a final or terminal bonus on
the maturation of the policy (also known as “with profits policies”).
176. The Commission is concerned that life insurance with an investment
component may be purchased by customers who do not fully understand that
they are long-term products. One of the ways in which this risk can be reduced
is through adequate disclosure of the features of the product, including its
objectives and the principal risks associated with the products. Paragraph 80
therefore specifies enhanced disclosure requirements for these products that
may be complied with either in the Policy Summary required under
paragraph 77 or in separate documentation provided with the Policy
Summary. The disclosure requirements, which are in addition to those set out
in paragraph 77 are considered in more detail in the paragraphs that follow:
90

177. Objectives: The Commission expects the objectives to include, as
appropriate:
(a) the insurance objectives;
(b) the return objectives, for example income (i.e., that the product aims to
pay the policyholder a regular income) or capital growth (i.e., that any
growth in value of the underlying assets, profits or income will
accumulate over the life of the product); and
(c) the investment objectives, for example to provide exposure to certain
markets or asset classes or to enable the policyholder to participate in
the profits of the insurer.
178. Suitability: Paragraph 77(3)(b) requires the Policy Summary or
accompanying document, to specify who the product is suitable for. This
could include, as appropriate that the product is only suitable for persons:
(a) who are prepared to commit to a long term/medium term investment
and who are unlikely to need access to their funds in the short/medium
term (an approximate timescale should be included);
(b) who are prepared to accept the risk that the value of their investment
may fall;
(c) who require the type of insurance cover provided (which should be
briefly explained).
179. Customer commitment: The commitment that the customer is making will
need to be clearly specified. For example, the commitment could be to make
a lump sum investment or to make regular monthly/annual or other periodic
investments. Any other commitments should be specified.
180. Material risks: The Commission considers that the material risks should
include, as appropriate:
(a) The investment risks. These are likely to include the general risk that
the benefits will depend on the performance of the underlying
investments and that investment returns are not guaranteed. However,
there may also be particular product specific risks depending on the
nature of the underlying investment, for example how broadly based it
is, whether the underlying investment is subject to significant
fluctuations etc.
(b) A clear statement that early termination may result in no or limited
benefits being provided under the policy and the loss of all investments
made, particularly if there is an early surrender fee.
(c) The returns may be insufficient to pay the administration and other fees.
(d) Unless the performance of the investments exceeds the rate of inflation,
the real value of the investment may reduce.
The above are just examples. A licensed insurer will need to ensure that all
material risks are set out.
181. Main features: The Commission expects licensed insurers to draft the
additional documentation in line with paragraph 77(2).
91

182. Charges: The Commission expects a licensed insurer to set out all the fees
and charges applicable to the policy, including any initial charge, the
management and administration fees, any early surrender charge, any
termination fee, the insurance charge (i.e., the premium payable for the life
cover), and any fees or charges.
183. Projections and past performance data: The Commission considers that the
provision of projections and past performance data constitutes a significant
business conduct risk, particularly with respect to retail customers. The
Commission expects licensed insurers to provide conservative projections
and to clearly set out the limitations of projections and past performance
data.
Retail customers
184. As already noted, retail customers usually have limited knowledge about
insurance as a financial product and their rights and obligations under
insurance contracts. The Commission expects a licensed insurer to take this
into account when it markets an insurance product directly to a retail
customer and, where appropriate, to provide additional information and
explanations to a retail customer. Matters on which additional explanations
may be required may include, for example
(a) the obligation to disclose fully any facts or matters that are material,
including (where appropriate) guidance on what type of facts or
matters may be considered material;
(b) the potential consequences for failing to disclose fully material facts or
matters;
(c) any obligations that must be complied with when an insurance contract
is concluded and while it is in force, and the consequences of non-
compliance; and
(d) cancellation rights, and any charges associated with early cancellation.
Provision of information on claims procedures
185. Paragraph 82(2) requires a licensed insurer to provide details of the claim
procedures together with the policy document. Given that, at this point, a
prospective policyholder has become a policyholder, the Commission expects
that the information provided will be more detailed than the summary
provided in the Policy Summary. In particular, the insurer should provide
guidance on the submission of claims. The guidance should advise the
policyholder of the obligation to notify the insurer of a loss as soon as it
occurs or as soon as it is reasonably practicable. The Insured(s) attention
should be drawn to the fact that prompt reporting of the loss is crucial for the
preservation of evidence that may be critical in determining admissibility and
the quantum of the claim.
92

Policy Servicing and Claims Handling
Policy servicing requirements
84. (1) A licensed insurer must
(a) service insurance contracts that it has sold appropriately through to
the point at which all its obligations under the insurance contract
have been satisfied;
(b) during the period in which an insurance contract is in force, disclose
to the policyholder information on
(i) any contractual changes to an insurance contract; and
(ii) any relevant changes to the insurer.
(2) If it proposes to make contractual changes to an insurance contract
during the term of the insurance contract, a licensed insurer must give the
policyholder notice of the proposed change.
(3) A notice under subparagraph (2) must
(a) inform the policyholder of the impact of the proposed change on the
rights and obligations of the policyholder;
(b) specify a period of time within which the policyholder may agree to
the change;
(c) notify the policyholder that, if the policyholder does not agree to the
change within the time period specified in the notice, the
policyholder will be taken to have rejected the proposed change.
(4) If a licensed insurer offers to renew an insurance contract on
different contractual terms, it must, at least 21 days before the renewal date
inform the policyholder in writing of
(a) the change to the contractual terms; and
(b) the impact of the contractual change on the rights and obligations of
the policyholder should the policyholder renew the insurance
contract.
Claims handling
85. (1) A licensed insurer must
(a) handle claims promptly, fairly and in a transparent manner;
(b) provide reasonable guidance to help a customer make a claim;
(c) provide information on the process for settling claims, including
expected timelines for the settlement of claims;
(d) investigate the claim expiditiously;
(e) provide a customer with information concerning the status of the
claim on an ongoing basis;
(f) not unreasonably reject a claim, including by terminating or
avoiding a policy;
(g) where appropriate, provide information on the basis for the rejection
or partial rejection of a claim;
93

(h) settle claims promptly once settlement terms are agreed;
(i) maintain a claims register in which the details of every insurance
claim made are recorded.
(2) Without limiting subparagraph (1), a licensed insurer must develop
and publish service level standards covering the claims handling process.
(3) A licensed insurer must ensure that a summary of its claims
procedures and claims payment procedures is displayed in each branch, contact
and agency office.
(4) The summary referred to in subparagraph (3), must include
information relevant to retail policyholders, including where appropriate, the
documents required to be submitted with a claim.
(5) If a claimant makes a claim outside the time period for the
submission of claims specified by the insurer, the insurer must not reject the
claim without ascertaining the reason for the claim being made late and
considering whether there are reasonable grounds for accepting the claim.
Claims Manual
86. (1) A licensed insurer must maintain a Claims Manual that sets out the
insurer’s policies and procedures for dealing with customer claims, established and
maintained in accordance with paragraph 65(3)(f).
(2) The policies and procedures for dealing with customer claims shall
(a) include procedures for ensuring compliance with paragraphs (a) to
(g) of paragraph 85(1);
(b) specify timelines for dealing with claims for different classes of
insurance business
(3) In setting timelines for dealing with claims, a licensed insurer must
take full account of the Guidelines issued by the Commission.
(4) A licensed insurer must ensure that an up-to-date copy of its Claims
Manual is filed with the Commission.
Life insurance contracts
87. (1) In the case of a life insurance contract with a maturity date, the insurer
must give the policyholder (or the life assured, as appropriate), not less than 2
months written notice of the maturity of the contract.
(2) A notice under subparagraph (1) must
(a) specify the maturity date;
(b) provide details of the entitlement to benefits on maturity and the
amount payable;
(c) set out any requirements with respect to payment; and
(d) be accompanied by a discharge form
(3) If a policyholder or life assured under an endowment policy or any
other life policy that has a surrender value requests the insurer for a surrender
value, the insurer must provide, with the surrender value, information on any
other options that may be available as an alternative to surrendering.
94

(4) A life insurer must maintain a schedule of all unpaid maturity claims,
with a note as to the reason for non-payment.
(5) The claims handling procedures, service level standards and claims
manual must include maturity claims.
Complaints policy and procedures and the handling of complaints
88. (1) A licensed insurer must
(a) establish and maintain a complaints policy and procedures which
provide for the effective consideration and proper handling of any
complaints made to it and for appropriate remedial action to be
taken, where appropriate; and
(b) maintain a complaints register in which the insurer must record any
complaints received together with details of how the complaint has
been, or is being dealt with.
(2) A licensed insurer must
(a) respond to complaints promptly, fairly and in a transparent manner;
and
(b) provide a complainant with information concerning the handling of
the complaint, and keep the complainant updated concerning
progress.
(3) The complaints policies and procedures must include complaints
made to the insurer against intermediaries when acting in relation to the
insurer’s products.
(4) A licensed insurer must ensure that a summary of its complaints
handling procedures is displayed in each branch, contact and agency office.
Significant complaints
89. (1) Subject to subparagraph (2), a “significant complaint” is a complaint that
alleges
(a) a breach of the Act, the Regulations or the directives;
(b) bad faith, malpractice or impropriety on the part of the licensed
insurer or one of its directors, employees or agents;
(c) the repetition or recurrence of a matter previously complained of,
whether significant or otherwise; or
(d) that the complainant has suffered, or may suffer, financial loss that
is material in relation to his or her financial circumstances.
(2) A complaint must not be treated as significant if it relates to a minor
clerical error.
(3) A significant complaint must be considered by a senior manager of
the licensed insurer who is independent of the circumstances that gave rise to
the complaint.
(4) If a significant complaint remains unsettled for longer than two
months, the licensed insurer must immediately inform the Commission and
must also advise the complainant that he or she may inform the Commission
directly of the complaint.
95

(5) If a licensed insurer has given a substantive response in relation to a
significant complaint, unless and until the insurer has received an indication
from the complainant that the response is unsatisfactory, the insurer is entitled
to treat the complaint as settled and resolved after the expiry of four weeks
from the date of its response.
(6) Subparagraph (5) does not affect any rights that the complainant has
in relation to matters on which the complaint is based and does not prevent the
complainant responding to the licensed insurer concerning the complaint after
the four-week period has expired.
(7) The first substantive reply to a significant complaint must, unless it
offers a settlement reasonably expected to be acceptable to the complainant,
advise the complainant that he or she has a right to complain directly to the
Commission.
GUIDELINES
Policy servicing requirements
186. Contractual changes to an insurance contract that require disclosure under
paragraph 84(1)(b)(i) could include, for example, a premium increase (where
permitted), to adjust for inflation.
The Commission:
(a) considers that a licensed insurer would not have any power to change
the terms of an insurance contract, after it is effected, unless permitted
to do so by the contract; and
(b) is unlikely to approve a policy containing such a term unless it is
reasonable and fair.
187. Relevant changes to a licensed insurer that require disclosure under
paragraph 84(b)(ii) could include
(a) changes in the name of the insurer;
(b) changes in the address of the head office of the insurer and, in the case
of specific policyholders, any branches that the policyholder may
reasonably use;
(c) any changes in the legal status of the insurer, whether as a result of
mergers or acquisitions or otherwise;
(d) any relevant portfolio transfers.
96

Claims procedures and handling
188. Paragraph 65(3)(f) requires that the business conduct procedures of a
licensed insurer include procedures for dealing with customer claims in a fair
and timely manner. The Commission expects the claims procedures to cover
all stages in the handling of a claim from the claim being raised to settlement
or rejection. The Commission also expects the claims procedures to include
expected timeframes, subject to extension in complex or exceptional cases.
189. Paragraph 85(1)(b) requires a licensed insurer to provide reasonable
guidance to help a customer make a claim. The Commission expects claim
forms, accident report forms and other claims documentation to be
straightforward and user friendly. The claims form should also include:
(i) details of the expected time frames for the various stages in the
consideration and settlement of claims; and
(ii) the contact details of the Commission for the purposes of lodging a
complaint with the Commission.
190. If a licensed insurer receives notification of a claim verbally, the insurer
should notify the claimant of the need to follow up in writing. Depending on
the insurer’s claims procedures and the nature of the claim, this may be by
letter, a completed claim form or a completed accident report form.
191. A licensed insurer should, when acknowledging a claim, notify the claimant
of any documents or information that it requires, or that will assist it, to
process the claim.
192. Licensed insurers should require intermediaries to provide any claims
received to pass them immediately to the insurer.
193. Paragraph 85(1)(c) requires a licensed insurer to provide a customer with
information concerning the status of the claim on an ongoing basis. In the
case of a straightforward claim, this may entail no more than acknowledging
that a claim has been received and providing details of the insurer’s decision
on the claim. However, in the case of complex or exceptional claims, where
the time period to resolution is likely to be extended, the Commission would
expect an insurer to provide one or more interim status reports.
194. Paragraph 85(1)(d) requires a licensed insurer to investigate claims
expeditiously. The Commission expects that, if the insurer does not have
sufficient expertise to fully investigate the claim, it will appoint an expert to
assist it with the investigation.
195. Paragraph 85(5) provides that if a claimant makes a claim outside the time
period for the submission of claims specified by the insurer, the insurer must
not reject the claim without ascertaining the reason for the claim being made
late. For example, a claim may have been made late due to circumstances
beyond the control of the claimant . Insurers have a duty to treat their
customers fairly and the Commission considers that, regardless of the
contractual position, an insurer should consider whether there are grounds
or extenuating circumstances that justify accepting a late claim.

198. Paragraph 65(3)(f) also requires that the business conduct procedures of a

no grounds for a complaint. The disagreement on which the dispute is based
may be a disagreement concerning the facts or a legal point. Alternatively,
even where a licensed insurer accepts a claim in full, the policyholder may
have a legitimate complaint, for example over the process or the time taken
to decide the claim. Of course, a dispute may also involve a complaint. It is
important the business conduct procedures distinguish between disputes and
complaints.
199. The Commission expects a licensed insurer to establish clear,
straightforward and transparent dispute procedures that enable disputes to
be considered fairly and promptly. The Commission also expects licensed
insurers to consider setting up procedures enabling an internal review of
disputed claims decisions by different persons to those who made the original
decision. It is in the interests of both customers and insurers to avoid a
reference to the Commission’s Complaints Bureau as this is likely to increase
costs.

concerning each claim, including the basis of the claim and the stages of the
claim through to its resolution. The Register should also record any
application to the Commission’s Complaints Bureau, and the ultimate
resolution of the claim. The Commission expects licensed insurers to keep
copies of all documentations provided to claimants and to document how
claims have been settled and why.

205. The loss of a policy document is inconvenient, but not crucial, as the policy
is not the contract itself, merely evidence of it. In the event that a policy
document has been lost, a life insurer should undertake a search and make
enquiries from anyone who might hold the policy or know of its whereabouts,
for example, the assured's bankers, solicitors, or accountants.
206. If the policy is not found, and the insurer is satisfied that the policy is
genuinely lost, it may ask the claimant to execute a Statutory Declaration,
setting out the circumstances of the loss and stating that the policy has not
been assigned or charged. The claim can then be paid on completion of an
indemnity from the claimant, executors, trustees, beneficiaries (as
appropriate) against any losses to the insurer as a result of making payment
without production of the policy. An indemnity cannot prevent a further claim
by an assignee; it can only repay the insurer any loss incurred thereby.
Similar procedures will apply to other lost documents of title, for example,
deeds of assignment.
Complaints
207. The Commission expects a licensed insurer to monitor complaints that it
receives in relation to or involving any insurance intermediaries that have
distributed insurance contracts on its behalf. This may enable an insurer to
identify issues with specific insurance intermediaries or highlight
improvements that could be made to training and/or product information.
208. Licensed insurers should also analyse complaints with a view to identifying
specific trends or recurring risks as this may enable insurers, for example, to
improve procedures or staff training.
Relationship with Intermediaries
Conducting business with insurance intermediaries
90. (1) A licensed insurer must not conduct business with an insurance
intermediary unless it is satisfied that
(a) the intermediary is licensed under the Act or, if applicable, an
appropriate exemption is in place; and
(b) the person is competent to conduct the business which is the subject
of the agreement.
(2) A licensed insurer must ensure that any business that it conducts with
an insurance intermediary is covered by a written agreement that
(a) sets out the respective responsibilities of the licensed insurer and the
insurance intermediary;
(b) promotes the fair treatment of customers; and
(c) in the case of an insurance agent, complies with paragraph 91(1).
(3) A licensed insurer must establish, maintain and implement
procedures and controls that enable it to have effective oversight of the conduct
and activities of its insurance agents.
101

(4) A licensed insurer must not conduct business with an insurance
intermediary whose shareholder, director, officer or employee serves as a
shareholder, director, officer or employee of such a licensed insurer.
Appointment of insurance agents
91. (1) A licensed insurer that appoints an insurance agent must make the
appointment through a written insurance agency agreement that includes
(a) the terms and conditions of the appointment;
(b) the scope of the agent’s authority, in relation to insurance contracts
that may be distributed, functions that may be performed and actions
that may be undertaken, as agent;
(c) any limitations on the agent’s authority;
(d) the rights, responsibilities and duties of the agent and of the licensed
insurer;
(e) the procedures for the handling and remittance of premiums
collected by the agent;
(f) provision for monitoring the agent’s performance of the insurance
agency agreement;
(g) the basis for the remuneration of the agent;
(h) provision for the termination of the agreement by both the licensed
insurer and the agent, including the entitlement of the agent, if any,
to future commission payments; and
(i) provisions for the resolution of disputes between the parties.
(2) A licensed insurer must keep a register of all insurance agents that it
has appointed which must
(a) contain the full name, business address and contact details of each
agent; and
(b) record
(i) the date upon which the agent was appointed and on which the
appointment was terminated; and
(ii) the policies and products for which the agent is authorised.
GUIDELINES
Agreement with intermediaries
209. An insurance intermediary, when acting for an insurer, often has a client
facing role and the way in which the insurance intermediary conducts its
business will therefore have a significant impact on the fair treatment of
customers. Although a licensed insurance intermediary has responsibilities
under the Act and the Insurance Intermediary Directive with respect to the
fair treatment of its own customers, the licensed insurer and the intermediary
102

should ensure that the agreement between them promotes the fair treatment
of, as appropriate, the clients of the insurer and the intermediary.
210. The directive sets out the requirements for an insurance agency agreement.
An agreement with any other type of insurance intermediary should cover, as
far as relevant and appropriate, matters such as:
 product development
 product promotion
 the provision of pre-contractual and point of sale information to
customers
 policy servicing
 claims notification and handling
 complaints notification and handling
 information to be provided to the insurer, including management
information
 remedial measures
 matters relating to the relationship with customers.
Training
Training obligations
92. (1) A licensed insurer must provide appropriate training to
(a) any of its employees who have responsibilities in relation to the
distribution of insurance contracts; and
(b) any insurance agents appointed to act in relation to the distribution
of its insurance contracts.
(2) The training provided in accordance with subparagraph (1) must
(a) include appropriate and relevant training on
(i) relevant provisions of the Act, the Regulations or the directives;
(ii) the duties and responsibilities of the employee or agent in
relation to the distribution of insurance contracts;
(iii) the specific insurance contracts and products that the employee
or agent will be authorised to distribute;
(iv) the Ghana insurance market;
(v) changes to the policies and products of the licensed insurer; and
(vi) consumer protection and the fair treatment of customers and
prospective customers;
(b) be tailored to the procedures and controls of the licensed insurer and
its insurance contracts and products;
(c) provide the employee or agent with sufficient technical knowledge
to explain the policies and products to customers and prospective
policyholders.
103

(3) Training under this paragraph must be provided to agents and
employees as soon as practicable after their appointment and on an ongoing
basis.
(4) Without limiting subparagraph (3), product training must be
provided at least annually.
GUIDELINES
Training
211. Paragraph 92 requires a licensed insurer to provide appropriate training to
those of its employees who have responsibilities in relation to the distribution
of insurance contracts, and its agents.
212. It should be noted that an insurance agent is not, and cannot be, an employee
of the insurer. The training provided should recognise this as there are
certain differences between the functions of an employee and of an insurance
agent with respect to the selling and distribution of insurance and with
respect to their relationship with the insurer.
104
